speechtext:
House again in Committee on Bill (No. 128) to authorize a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.-Mr. Fielding.
On section 1,

The hon. the Minister of Finance said yesterday that they did not purpose making a loan for ten years, but the chances were they would make a long loan for 25 years or 30 years, or perhaps 50 years. His remarks would lead to the conclusion that he has no hope that the Grand Trunk Pacific will pay off this loan at the termination of the ten years. Now, look at the thing from a business standpoint. Would any business man make a loan at a high rate when he did not intend to use the money? If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance collects the amount of this loan from the Grand Trunk Pacific at the end of the ten years, as he intends doing, he should simply make a loan covering that period. Then, when he is repaid by the Grand Trunk Pacific, he will pay off that loan ; and if he requires more money, he would borrow at a lower rate. He says' that this loan which he intends making in order to obtain the funds for the Grand Trunk Pacific, will be at four per cent or perhaps a little more. Looking back, I find that in 1895 and 1896 my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) who was then Finance Minister, floated loans at about 2J per cent. Canada was then passing through a period of depression, which should have made the loan dearer, yet, n'otwithstanding the good times we have had since, my hon. friend has succeeded in lowering the credit of Canada to that extent that he has to pay four per cent for money, as compared with 21 per cent paid by his predecessor. And this money which he requires to borrow, to hand over to the Grand Trank Pacific, and which the Grand Trunk Pacific agree tc repay in ten years, he purposes borrowing on a long term. Would it not be much more businesslike to borrow the money for ten years and then when repaid by the Grand Trunk Pacific pay off that loan. By that time the interest rate will in all probability be lower; and should he require more money, he would be able to borrow it at less than four per cent. But by his present policy, he is about to bind himself to pay four per cent during 25, 30 or even 50 years. Suppose for instance, a property owner wanted to raise some more money on his property, but found it difficult to get advances from money lenders because his property was already subject to first, second and third mortgages. He however goes to a neighbour who has money to lend and who also owns property

and says to him: 'If you will go to the money market and borrow the $10,000 I require, which you can do on more favourable terms than I can, I will in return give you the security of my property for an advance of the same amount.' The transaction is put through in each case for ten years. At the end of that term, the one who borrowed in the money market will repay his loan with the money obtained by him from the second borrower; and then if he should require other money, he would borrow it at a lower rate. He might in that time be able to borrow at 2i per cent. But the government proposes to go on paying four per cent for 25, 30 or 50 years, instead of making a ten year loan at four per cent, and then if necessary reborrowing at a lower rate.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have to dissent entirely from the statements of my hon. friend, in so far as they imply that any loans have been placed by this government on terms otherwise than favourable, having regard to the conditions of the money market at the time the loans weTe issued. An argument which does not take account of these conditions is absurd. You cannot make a loan at a better rate than the conditions of the market at the time warrant. Suppose a buyer for one of the great houses is sent abroad to purchase goods. When he returns his employer says to him: 'I see that you bought goods at one and six per yard which some years ago you bought at one and three per yard. You have therefore failed in your duty to your firm.' Would not a satisfactory answer be: 'I bought the goods at the best rate I could at the time.' Well, in buying money, as in buying dry goods, you have to pay what the market demands. You are governed in both cases by the conditions of the market. Judged by that test, which is the only true one, every loan made by this government is a satisfactory one. If it be found necessary to make compai isons between the loans floated by my predecessors and those floated during my retention of the office, I am confident there will be nothing in the comparison which will in the slightest degree reflect on the policy of the present government; and in saying this, I do not wish to criticise in the slightest the actions of my predecessors. who no doubt got the best prices they could at the time and under the conditions then existing. With regard to the policy of restricting the government to the issue of a 10 year loan, to cover this advance, I do not think that would be wise. It is possible that the conditions of the market may be such as to render it desirable that we should issue a 10-year loan, and in that case I would hold myself free to do so. 1 Mr. G. TAYLOR.
hope, however, it will be otherwise. A short term loan necesarily implies, in most cases, a higher rate of interest than a long term. Whenever it becomes necessary for us to borrow, our duty is to have regard to the conditions of the money market, and issue the loan on the best terms, at the best rate, and for the best period that will meet the existing conditions. I would object just as much to a proposal to limit the loan to a 25 or 50 year period as to the proposal to limit it to a 10 year period. So much with regard to the first two points. As to the third point, although it does not add anything to the argument, it may surprise my hon. friend to know that we are pursuing the same course as that which was pursued by the late government in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway loan. That loan was made for some five or six years. Immediately after it was agreed upon, the then Minister of Finance had to go on the money market and he placed on that market a loan-for what term? Five or six years? No. He made it for fifty years with the option of redeeming it at the end of 25 years.
What was the rate of that loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am very glad my hon. friend has put that question. They lent the money to the Canadian Pacific Railway at a fixed rate of interest, four per cent, as we propose to do to the Grand Trunk Pacific. and then went into the money market and paid more than four per cent for the money. So they pursued exactly the same policy as I am asking the House to approve. If it should happen that we will be obliged to pay a fraction more than four per cent, we shall be having the same experience as my predecessor.
Does the hon. minister approve of the plan pursued in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was not here at that time; but looking back, I do not hesitate to say that I am glad the government lent the Canadian Pacific Railway that money. There was a difference of opinion at the time regarding that policy. Better men than I thought it was not wise, but they have possibly since changed their views. It is easy to be wise after the event, and the men who were in parliament then had to determine the question according to the best light they had at the moment. And many of that day thought it was not a wise plan. I express no opinion except to say that in view of the great success of the Canadian Pacific Railway, there is none of us, I hope, who would not be willing to say, on looking back upon it, that we are glad the government gave them that aid. I say that, at all events, speaking for myself." So, the hon. gentlemen will see that

on every point of criticism of this loan, I can cite the precedent of the Canadian Pacific Railway loan. I do not attach much importance to that, but it is quite proper that, as a matter of illustration, 1 should refer to it. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that we are going to receive only 4 per cent and that the loan will cost us more. That was exactly the condition of the case with the Canadian Pacific Railway loan, and, as a matter of fact, in the case of that loan the rate of interest paid for the money was somewhat over 4 per cent. The hon. gentleman asks why we do not seek a short term ten year loan. Well, my predecessors did not think it was wise to do this in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway loan. They held their hands free, they went into the market and found what the condition was, they adapted their loan to that condition, and, no doubt, they got the money at the best price at which it could be obtained. I mention this, not as an accusation against those who made the Canadian Pacific Railway loan, but as it may help to illustrate the present transaction. But I do not think that argument necessary to the case. I maintain that this loan is a fair business proposition, and that it ought to commend itself to the judgment of the House.

The ground of my complaint is that the Finance Minister is anticipating that, ten years from now, he will not be able to make a loan at less than four per cent, notwithstanding the progress of the country in the meantime, which he looks forward to so hopefully. He seems to think that the credit of the country will be so bad in ten years from now that he will look to the railway company to refund the money, and he will use it for the balance of the term of the loan. If we are to have the great progress and the good time that he anticipates on account of the building of this railway, we ought to be able to borrow ten millions in ten years from now at 2i per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then, my predecessors must have
Never mind your predecessors. You are doing business now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am doing business, true. But in this case, I am not comparing myself with my predecessors to their disadvantage. I am saying that, as far as I can see, they acted as reasonable business men. I am commending them. I see nothing in that transaction to-day that was not proper and businesslike. Nor have I said anything to suggest the contrary. We are pursuing the same businesslike course that they pursued. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Geo. Taylor) says that we are
anticipating that we shall not be able to borrow at less than 4 per cent in ten years. That might have been applied to the Canadian Pacific Railway loan in its time. At the expiration of ten years, when the money is repaid, it is reasonably probable the government of Canada will still require money for its public purposes, and the situation then will be that, instead of being obliged to go out and float some new loans to meet the demands of that moment, we shall have $10,000,000 in the treasury. So, I do not think there is any cause of criticism from that standpoint.

I have not yet heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) any convincing or satisfactory answer to the question submitted from this side of the House as to whether it would not be better, in fixing the terms of this loan, to provide that the borrower should pay to the government exactly what it might cost the government to make the loan. An attempt has been made to answer that, but it does not seem to me to be satisfactory or to meet the case. Now, this loan has become necessary owing to the stress of circumstances pressing upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. In other words, the government is coming to the assistance of the railway, as one might put it, as a matter of charity, and, at the same time, while the government is professing to do this charitable act, the Finance Minister tells us that the conditions of this contract are such that, if he has to pay a little more than four per cent for the money, the government will suffer the loss. At the same time, he says that if the government is able to borrow this money at a rate a shade less than four per cent, the country will be making a profit out of this loan. It does not strike me that the circumstances warrant the position taken by the Finance Minister. Would the Finance Minister feel quite comfortable with a profit made from this poverty-stricken offspring of the government jingling in the treasury? It seems to me that, in an act of charity, the government ought to get back-if it gets back anything-just what it paid, and, considering the care the government have taken to foster this child of theirs, that it would not be fair to take a profit won through an act of charity. It seems to me that it would be quite within the power of the government, and it would not be asking anything unfair from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Comqany, to insist that this contract should contain a condition that the railway company shall pay to the government just what it costs the government to make this loan. We do not want to make a profit out of the railway company in this matter. But we do not want to make a loss. It is quite possible, quite within the range of our

powers, to so provide in this contract that we shall neither make a loss nor make a profit. Would not that be a reasonable, fair and proper way to protect the rights of both parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I confess that, if we should make a profit out of this transaction -I have not said we shall, I have guarded against that-I am free to confess now that I shall probably have more comfort, speaking officially, in jingling the profit of the transaction in my official pocket than my predecessor had in pocketing the loss incurred in the former transaction. And, if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, in receiving this aid, is to be described as a ' poverty-stricken ' concern, and if this is to be described as 'an act of charity,' I suppose we shall have to say that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at the time of the loan made to it was a ' poverty-stricken ' concern, and the loan to them as ' an act of charity.' I would not apply those terms to either case. In each case, the loan is legitimate aid granted to a great enterprise. And when I show the hon. gentleman (Mr. Porter) that, in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway it was deemed wise to fix a definite rate of interest, as we are doing, I do not ask him to accept that as a conclusive argument, but I cite it as showing that at least the men of that day and the men of this, dealing with a business transaction, thought alike and acted alike.

That does not seem a very convincing argument. If, in the light of subsequent events, the loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is shown to be improper or wrong, or not on the best terms that could have been obtained, why should the Minister of Finance use that loan for an argument in committing that wrong a second time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say it was right.

But my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) would not say that in answer to a question put a few minutes ago. He has not expressed an opinion upon that, but left that to the expression of opinion that had been given years ago. If it was wrong in that instance-and the minister will not say it was right-why will he invoke that as an argument for a repetition of the act? It is reducing the argument to this: two wrongs make a right. And he is going to commit the second wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Except that I have not said it was wrong.

Has the minister made any effort to obtain money outside the London brokers? My reason for asking is, that, in looking over the finances of the United States, I find that they have a total debt of $913,000,000, of which $118,400,000 is at four per cent, $63,900,000 at three per cent, Mr PORTER.
and the balance at two per cent. I believe I am correctly informed that the bonds floated by the United States in respect of the Panama canal pay only two per cent. I cannot quite understand why they can borrow so much cheaper than we can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will lcok into that matter, he will find that in the case of United States bonds, there are certain exemptions and privileges which give them special value. He will find also that the banks have to have certain classes of these bonds to deposit against their note circulation. All these things create a value for certain classes of United States bonds which would not apply to the bonds of any other country. My hon. friend began by asking if I had made any efforts to borrow money outside London. We have no difficulty in borrowing money at current rates. Our loans as a rule are placed in London, because London is the cheapest money market of the world. We keep our eyes on other markets, of which we have occasionally availed ourselves to make temporary loans, and we are not unmindful of conditions in the United States. At times when there seemed to be an abundance of money in the United States, I have inquired, and I have always found that if we attempted to issue our loans in the United States the charges against them would make the expense of the transaction very considerable, and the net result would be less favourable than we were able to obtain at the same time in London. Indeed, in many cases when United States bankers and others take up foreign loans, what actually happens is that while the transaction nominally takes place in the United States, the bonds are placed in London, and they are sold and bought on the basis of the London prices. I can assure my hon. friend that though occasional conditions, according to the newspapers, might show that for certain purposes and under special circumstances money is cheap in the United States, it is safe to say that for the purposes of large loan transactions, London is to-day, as it has been for a great many years, the cheapest money market in the world.

I can understand why the banks of the United States should have some advantages, but I cannot see why we should be paying double the amount the United States are paying on a similar loan. When you see them paying only two per cent on $700,000,000 you cannot but feel that in some way we are paying a higher rate of interest than they are paying in proportion.

What I am particularly interested in is to find out how this $10,000,000 is to be applied. I tried to get an explanation from the Finance Minister the other day, and he stated that he would carefully guard the payment of that

money and see that it was paid on progress estimates. The statement that he brings down to the House is two-fold: An estimate is to be made by the engineer of the Railway Department for the purpose of the payment of some indebtedness to the extent of $7,100,000, and to finish the prairie section, an amount equal to $10,-
500,000.	The Grand Trunk Pacific, who are borrowing the money, only ask for $9,400,000, and in that statement there is a sum for the purpose of recouping them, a payment which they allege to have made of $7,100,000. The Finance Minister says,
'I will carefully guard the payment of this sum of money to the railway company by seeing that the work is done and completed.' But the work has been done and completed long ago, the money is paid to the parties who have done the work, and there is the certificate of our own engineer saying that the work is done. Then what do they want the $7,100,000 for? It is an alleged indebtedness which, he says, the Grand Trunk Company advanced to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Well, we all know the absurdity of it, we all know that the Grand Trunk had not $5 to advance, that the corporation could not endorse even a security for that amount. Who is it we are going to pay the $7,100,000 to? It is to some loan that the Grand Trunk Pacific have made, or a sum of money equal to $7,100,000 which they must have borrowed from some bank. We ought to have full particulars, we ought to have an accurate account of the payment of that $7,100,000. We do not know, by any statement that has been made by the Finance Minister, to whom we owe this $7,100,000 or whom we are going to pay it to. We have his statement that he will take care that no part of that sum is paid out unless on progress estimates on the work. The sum is paid out, the work has been done by the contractors, there is no progress estimates to come in, there is the certificate of his I own engineer that the work is done and the money is paid out. Now surely this committee is entitled to this information. To whom is that $7,100,000 to be paid, and in what form was that advance to the Grand Trunk Pacific? Was it advanced solely on account of woTk or in the construction of the prairie section and for no other purpose? That information this committee is entitled to in detail. We are advancing a sum of $10,000,000, $7,100,000 to pay an advance of some kind. The details of that advance we have not got up to the present moment; and this committee, before voting that money, is surely entitled to a detailed account.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Wei are not going to vote that sum of money to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, we are not going to vote that $7,100,000 to any company.
To whom are you going to vote it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not going to vote that particular sum to anybody, we have nothing to do with that particular sum. What we have to do is to see that before we pay $1 of money raised by the aid of the government, we shall have a certificate of the engineer that that money has been expended on the road, and we have the work there before us. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, instead of borrowing money from a bank to pay its contractors, have been able to go to the coffers of the Grand Trunk Company itself, it is their own business, and we are not concerned in it at all. Whether they got the money from the treasury of the Grand Trunk or whether they got it from a bank, is of no importance to us. I presume that had they not got that money from some quarter, we would have a cry all over the land that a great many workmen were being unpaid, that merchants were being unpaid. My hon. friend speaks of the work having been certified. The work has not been certified for the purpose of any payment. We have the estimate of our engineers as to what amount will be necessary; we have statements made by the Grand Trunk Company of what amount is required to finish the road, and our engineers say that that is substantially correct.
You say the work has not been certified by your own engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not as respects the payment of any money. If $7,000,000 drawn from a bank, or from another Tailway company, or from any other quarter, have gone into that work, and certificates are brought to us by our engineers that that money has gone into the work, then we are justified in responding by paying out of the funds the proper proportion of the money. My hon. friend will find that that advance to the Grand Trunk Company is practically in the same position as if one of the banks had advanced the money. We are not called upon to consider whether the company was right or not to advance it; that is none of our business. What we are concerned in is seeing that not one dollar of this money is paid except on certificates of our own engineers that it is based upon actual outlays, and that the money has gone into the work. That is provided, not upon any assertion of mine, but it is provided by the machinery in the schedule attached to this Act. I would like my hon. friend to get out of his mind this idea that we are going to pay the Grand Trunk Railway $7,000,000. If the Grand Trunk Pacific had borrowed $7,000,000 from a bank, we would not be concerned about that. We are going to pay the money, under the



terms of the contract, to the Grand Trunk Pacific upon evidence that that amount of money has gone into the work. Now that is simple and I am sure that my hon. friend on reflection, will see that it is fair and reasonable.
You have the information already that the money has gone into the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has not been paid yet.

You have a statement from the Grand Trunk that they have advanced $7,100,000 and you could not pay the proceeds of the bonds for the construction of the work until you had the certificates from your own engineer. A statement has been submitted by your own engineer as to the correctness of the accounts. He submits a statement which completely confirms the statement of the company. The officer of the Department of Railways and Canals who has gone down to examine the accounts of the Grand Trunk Pacific certifies to them as being correct. Why is it that we cannot have the information showing us in what form the Grand Trunk are claiming a return of this $7,100,000? You do not go over the work again and you do not get a new certificate from your engineers. You have a certificate already that the work has been done and completed. You have paid the money for that work to a certain extent. That is as far as the $7,100,000 is concerned. It is true that you will require fresh certificates for the balance that you paid out of the $10,000,000 for the completion of the work. I believe the government are acting as trustees, that they have on hand a certain sum of money and that the balance of $10,000,000, after the $7,100,000 has been paid, is intended to complete the prairie section. But, as far as this $7,000,000 is concerned, that is a completed transaction. You have the certificate of the engineers as to the completion of the work. The amount has been paid and the accounts have been audited by the Department of Railways and Canals. Surely we are entitled to a statement as to who holds that indebtedness and in what form the payment of that $7,100,000 was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that I have not succeeded in satisfying my hon. friend.
I maintain very respectfully, in view of his larger knowledge and experience, that we are not concerned about that $7,100,000 at all. An hon. gentleman opposite asked the question what amount the Grand Trunk Company have, in one form ot another, put into this enterprise and we have the information brought down that they have put in $7,000,000. If they have put $7,000,000 in they stand in the same position as the Bank of Montreal would stand if it had loaned the Grand Trunk Pacific Company

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
$7,000,000. What concern would we have
in that?

I will tell my hon. friend what concern you have in that. Suppose it were part of the expenses of lobbying here and of the amount that was entered in an account which was considered by the Public Accounts Committee and the papers in regard to which were lost. Suppose one of these items was included in that account or something similar to it, have we not the right to see the account? When you come here and ask for $10,000,000 of which $7,100,000 has been paid out, have we not the right to know in what form this money has been paid out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite admit that my hon. friend ought to have a better knowledge than I have as to the expenses of lobbying and things of that kind, but I still insist that we are not asking to pay $7,000,000 to the Grand Trunk, and it is not open to us to enter into an inquiry as to how they used the money or as to what they did with the $7,000,000. They stand exactly in the position of a bank which had loaned the Grand Trunk Pacific Company for the purpose of its undertaking that .much money. We would have nothing to do with that. That would be a matter between the company and the bank. In this instance it is a matter between one company and another. Whether the Grand Trunk borrowed it, or loaned their credit are interesting questions in themselves, but they do not touch this loan. We are concerned in seeing what becomes of this money which we propose to lend to the company, and we have provided by this Bill that not one dollar of this money can be paid to the Grand Trunk Pacific until we receive the certificates from the engineer that the money has gone into the work and is represented by work to be seen.

We, on behalf of the
country, promised to give aid in the shape of a guarantee or other assistance. The balance was to be provided by the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk had to stand at their back and raise the balance of the money. We have lived up to our portion of the agreement. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway now come here and ask for an additional loan to help to build the road. But they say that $7,000,000 out of the $10,000,000 is required to pay back to the Grand Trunk Company because they advanced that amount. It was their duty to advance it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It was their duty to provide the security that would raise it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Yes, it was the understanding that they would advance that

money or that they would be at the back of the Grand Trunk Pacific and assist them to carry through the undertaking. They advanced a sum of money and now they turn around and ask us to advance more in order that this $7,000,000 may be paid back to them. I think we should say to them: 'It is true that you have advanced $7,000,000 to build this road, but that is what you ought to do, and if you have done that we are under no obligation to raise money to pay that amount back to you. We want you to carry out your part of the bargain.' They are doing no more than carrying out their paTt of the bargain and we are doing all we could be expected to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The error in my hon. friend's statement is that he says that the Grand Trunk were bound to advance this money.
JSTo, I did not put it that way, but I said that it was understood that they were to be at the back of the Grand Trunk Pacific and to provide the money by putting up the security or otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, my hon. friend's statement was that they were bound to advance the money and that they had a right to do it.
I did not say to advance the money; I said to be at their back and to furnish the security to aid in raising the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We must distinguish between these two things. The Grand Trunk never contemplated that out of its earnings it would take $7,000,000 and put it into this road. The Grand Trunk never .agreed to advance a dollar to this company. The Grand Trunk agreed to do exactly what it is proposing to do now ; that it would guarantee certain bonds of the western division. It has agreed to do that and it is not shirking that responsibility. It is willing and ready to do that and this legislation requires the company to do it, but, for financial reasons we think it best that the company should not float its guarantee in the present condition of the money market. If the Grand Trunk was bound to advance this $7,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and did not do so, and now asked us to do it, there would be something in what the hon. gentleman says, but that is not the situation at all. What the Grand Trunk agreed to do it is still doing by way of a guarantee of those bonds.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We could not assent for a moment to the statement just made by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. He says that the Grand Trunk were to guarantee the bonds, not for the balance but for some certain amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not say that. I was trying to show the distinction between 1664
a pledge to advance money and a pledge to guarantee bonds. I was not dealing with the question of the bonds.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) simply stated to the Finance Minister that the Grand Trunk were bound to guarantee the bonds necessary to raise the balance required for the completion of the western division.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understood the Minister of Finance to take direct issue with my hon. friend upon that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Well, I was very unfortunate in my understanding of what the hon. gentleman said. There is no doubt whatever as to what the contract was:
Inasmuch as the bonds to ibe guaranteed by the government only make provision for a I art of tbo cost of construction of the western division, the company hereby agrees that the Grand Trunk Railway Company af Canada shall guarantee bonds of the company for the balance required for the construction of said western division, exclusive of the said $20 000,000 required for first equipment, which the company is required to provide under paragraph 22 of this agreement.
The Grand Trunk Railway Company was to guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific for the balance required for the construction of the western division; that is the balance remaining after the provision made by the government on its guarantee of bonds, and there is no doubt my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) was strictly correct in the point he made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Railway did agree to do that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Grand Trunk Railway Company entered into an agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry out that condition of the contract, so that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) to argue that the Grand Trunk Railway was bound to advance the money, that they have advanced it, and now they are trying to get it back. My hon. friend, however, has made it clear now that such was not his argument.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
They are required to give that guarantee and the government is becoming banker.
Mr. FIELDING Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And they are getting back their $7,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has no relation to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the difference is accounted for by the equipment bonds which represent a very considerable sum.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I may be very ignorant as to what is correct procedure in these matters, but, to use the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway for providing equipment five years in advance of the time it will be required, and then to put that forward as an excuse for aid from the government seems a remarkably unbusinesslike proposition. Every one who has eyes in his head knows that some of this equipment has been continuously* in use on the Grand Trunk Railway system during the past two or three years, and yet we have it gravely put forward by Mr. Hays as a reason why the government should come to the assistance of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, that a guarantee has been given to equipment which has been used not on the Grand Trunk Pacific but on the Grand Trunk Railway system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a distinct provision with respect to the equipment bonds, and I do not see what relation that could have to the merits of the present case. I should think it would not be wise for the Grand Trunk Pacific to wait until the road was completed to look around for equipment. If all goes well a good part of that equipment will be needed for the operation of the road next season, and although I have no information on the point I take it for granted that if any car constructed Mr. FIELDING.
for the Grand Trunk Pacific and not immediately used was loaned to the Grand Trunk Railway Company or any other, they would give in return the usual business consideration to the Grand Trunk Pacific for it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Unless the Grand Trunk Pacific Company saw they could come to some such source as this for assistance I do not think they would engage in any such unbusinesslike methods. It was perfectly proper that they should provide their equipment in good time, but it does not seem reasonable that they should provide it two or three years in advance and use it on a railway system for which it was not designed at all. There was no expectation in the minds of the members of parliament who discussed the contracts of 1903 and 1904 that the guarantee stipulated for would be utilized for the purpose of providing equipment for the Grand Trunk Railway system in the meantime. Certainly nobody ever expected that it would be used as an argument for further assistance from the government, especially as the very company which has been enjoying the benefit of that equipment in the meantime was described in 1903 as being in and of the undertaking and forming the whole thing in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only relation between the two things is that the Grand Trunk Company in stating the amount of obligation it had itself incurred in this enterprise very naturally stated that it guaranteed these bonds. I would rather prefer to discover that the Grand Trunk Pacific had the rolling stock in good time than to discover that when they needed it there was not sufficient to handle the business. I do not see why we need worry ourselves very much as to whether they got the equipment in 1908 or 1910 in view of the fact that they are spending their own money and not ours on that part of the enterprise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If that is so it was absolutely irrelevant for Mr. Hays to introduce the statement into his letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was perfectly legitimate to state the extent to which the Grand Trunk Railway Company was pledging its credit to help this enterprise, and more especially as it has been stated in various quarters that the government was doing everything in the matter and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company was doing nothing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where was this equipment obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot say I am sure, but I know that a good deal of it was obtained in the province of Nova Scotia

because I have seen the cars bearing the well known name of Rhodes, Curry and Company.
It was not supplied in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That must have been because the man in Nova Scotia was willing to build it more cheaply. However, I am only speaking from recollection and I will be glad to get the information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think there was some company formed for the purpose of supplying the equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say, I am not aware of that.
Did not the Grand Trunk Pacific secure a great number of old cars from the Grand Trunk and have the name changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say, but as not one dollar of government money has gone into that I do not think we need worry much over it.

I understood there was a provision in the Act whereby a separate company could be organized to provide that equipment and the security would be in the form of a chattel mortgage on the equipment which would be repaid by the [DOT] earnings from the road when in operation. That was put forward as a distinct and important provision in the Bill, which would enable them_ to provide this equipment for the road without drawing on their credit to any great extent. If part of this guarantee by the Grand Trunk was for this purpose what becomes of the company that was to be organized to provide the equipment? How do we know how much has gone into equipment or where the equipment was purchased or the amount of equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there was any such rolling stock company.
There certainly was such a provision in the Act. I remember Mr. Osier saying it was a common and useful practice on railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Undoubtedly such a system is employed on some railways but it was not in this case.
Does the minister know how much of the $7,000,000 which the Grand Trunk Pacific borrowed from the Grand Trunk Railway has been paid out for actual expenditure on the road bed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are dealing entirely with construction and can only recognize payments for construction.

Then every dollar of this may be for money that has gone towards the purchase of equipment for the
Grand Trunk Pacific that the Grand Trunk are now using.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it be possible that that would happen, they never could get a dollar back under this Act.

If that is so it has taken to that extent the credit of the Grand Trunk from the Grand Trunk Pacific and has made it necessary for the Grand Trunk Pacific to come here for a further loan. If the Grand Trunk had not advanced this money to purchase rolling stock which they are now using at four per cent, irrespective of the cost of repairs and maintenance, it seems to me they would have $7,000,000 more to apply to the construction of the road bed and it would not be necessary to come here for a loan of $10,000,000.

Would the minister make it clear whether this $10,000,000 is all to be used on work yet to be done or materials yet to be supplied, or whether any part of it is to be used to pay for work already done or material already purchased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If any application were made for payment of money for work already done or materials already furnished as respects which they have already received money why certainly they could not get it, but if work has been done by advances from the Grand Trunk or from anybody else which has not passed into _ the accounts and been approved and certified by the engineer, unquestionably they would have a right to draw a portion of this money for that purpose.
I want to ascertain whether the whole $10,000,000 is to be used in payment of work done so that there will be nothing left to continue the line to the mountains..

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the Grand Trunk have advanced money and it has gone into the road they would have a right to recover from the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if $7,000,000 has thus been put into the road there would be only $3,000,000 available from this fund to continue the work.
Then is it the case that $7,000,000 may have been spent in construction and road bed for which my hon. friend has no report from his engineers?

Our engineers know the condition of the road. We know that considerable sums of money have gone into it as respects which the statement of the Grand Trunk is probably correct, but we must know that the work is done and must have the engineers certify it before money is paid oveT.

Does my hon. friend understand from the statement of the Grand Trunk that they have put $7,000,000 into

the road for which he has no report from his engineers? If the government have reports from their engineers they ought to know how much of that $7,000,000 has already been expended and how much of that expenditure has been reported on by the engineers. Is it possible the Finance Minister does not know within one, two, five or seven millions how much money they put in for which he has no report from his engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We chiefly require reports from our engineers when a demand is made on us for money. If the Grand Trunk Pacific say: 'We want you to pay so much money,' that is when we insist on the reports and certificate of the engineers. As respects the condition of our work generally the chief engineer has one or two officers along the road who are in constant touch with him and he is kept generally informed of the condition of the work; but we are only concerned from a financial point of view when the company come to us and want so much money. Then when they are to get that money from a particular fund with which we have anything to do, we must be satisfied that the work has been done and the money expended.
We ought to have the information asked for.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the information is not covered by what is before the House and my hon. friend will draw my attention more specifically to what is lacking I will endeavour to get it if it is within my reach.
I want a specific statement that this sum is to be expended upon the road bed or stations of the prairie sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
It cannnot be applied to the payment of any equipment of the road or anything of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I understand that not a dollar of this can be applied to any other purpose than the construction of the road on the prairie section. ,
In what section of the schedule is that provided?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will find that provision in the mortgage. I think on page 18.
The minister has said that the furnishing of money to the Grand Trunk Pacific in respect of equipment has nothing to do with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not quite say that.

If that is the case we are entitled to be assured that this money Mr. CROTHERS.
is not to be applied to a purpose with which we have nothing to do. We are entitled to know that $7,000,000 of the $10,000,000 is not going to pay for equipment which the Grand Trunk is bound to furnish to the Grand Trunk Pacific, but that the $7,000,000 will be actually expended, every dollar, on the road bed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say without hesitation that this money is designed, as my hon. friend will see by the mortgage, to assist in the construction, not the equipment, of the prairie section.
If it has been expended on rolling stock, then this company is asking for $7,000,000 sooner than it should, because they do not require it for the purpose for which it is supposed to be expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I give the assurance, without any equivocation, that not a dollar of this money can be applied to any other purpose than the construction of the prairie section, as provided in the mortgage.
That does not answer the question. The question is whether this money is to go in repayment of money which has been expended already for rolling stock with which we have nothing to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not a dollar of it can go for equipment. The equipment is provided for by a different method.
The hon. minister does not know how much of this $7,000,000 is to be used to pay the Grand Trunk Railway for the rolling stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not going to pay the Grand Trunk Railway one dollar We will pay the Grand Trunk Pacific, on the engineers' certificates, as much of this $10,000,000 as they can show has gone into construction and only into construction; and the $7,000,000, while it is an interesting item of information to the House, has actually no bearing upon this at all. For every dollar anybody claims, we must know it has gone into the construction of the prairie section and not for equipment or anything else will we pay it.

The difference is this. There may come a time when you may be able to get an engineer to certify that $7,000,000 more has been expended on the road than really has been. I want to know if that money has been expended now or whether you take the money from the Grand Trunk Pacific to pay the Grand Trunk Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are not going to hand the Grand Trunk Railway money for equipment or anything else. The Grand

Trunk Railway in that respect, practically act as the bankers of the subsidiary company. If the Grand Trunk Pacific get the $7,000,000 to help them out, whether they get it from the parent company or the bank or anywhere else is not a matter that concerns us, and it does not enter into our calculations as to the paying out of this money. Before any of this $10,000,000 can be paid the engineer must certify that it is represented by work gone into the road. The money for this road is drawn from two sources, in the first place, from the proceeds of the government guarantee, and in the second place from the proceeds of the Grand Trunk Railway guarantee, in certain proportions. Before we can establish these respective proportions, we must know what money has gone into the road or the total cost of construction. Having ascertained that, we assign to each of these funds its proper proportion; and before one dollar of the fund can be drawn out, we must have the certificate of the engineer that the work is there to represent it.

Suppose the Finance Minister sent out to-morrow his engineer to find out how much money has _ been expended in the road bed, and his engineer gave it as a certain amount and that all the moneys received by the Grand Trunk Pacific had been sufficient to pay that work up to date, and that the $7,000,000 would not be required until $7,000,000 more of work had been put into the road, would he be justified in handing that $7,000,000 over now to pay for future work. Does it not look as if the Grand Trunk Pacific were getting that $7,000,000 to pay for the equipment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As regards the equipment I can give the most positive assurance that nothing of the kind is contemplated or is possible under this agreement.

I find that in answers given by the Finance Minister to the leader of the opposition that there has been expended on the prairie section $27,031,000, and that there is yet to be expended on that section $5,166,000, and we have to pay the Grand Trunk Railway $7,000,000. That makes $12,200,000 to be paid on a loan of $10,000,000, Where are the other $2,000,000 to be had to complete the prairie section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not paying the Grand Trunk Railway that money at all.

While the Finance Minister has made it quite clear that it is not the intention of the government, ostentatiously and publicly, to hand over any cash to the Grand Trunk Railway for the rolling stock, possibly the same result is to be obtained in another way. If we take
the information given in this most instructive statement brought down by the Finance Minister, a couple of facts seem quite clear. The first is that the Grand Trunk Pacific had plenty of money to complete its work. If this $10,000,000 is sufficient to complete it, then they had enough, bet-cause they have spent $8,000,000 on rolling stock. If the Grand Trunk Pacific had been willing to go on and finish their road they apparently had enough money to do so. Would the thing not work out this way according to this statement? The Grand Trunk Pacific, having the money on hand to complete this road save pos-i sibly the difference between $8,000,000 and $10,000,000 said: 'No, we will not complete the road, but we will put this money into rolling stock which we do not require but which the Grand Trunk Railway require and which the Grand Trunk Railway would have to pay its own money for.' Then, they hand this $7,000,000 over to the Grand Trunk Railway to buy rolling stock, and then declare that the money went into the read bed. In this way the Grand Trunk Railway is able to take $8,000,000 of the Grand Trunk Pacific and put it into rolling stock, and then loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific at four per cent the money required for construction. If that Is wnat has been done, and if the Grand Trunk Railway comes and says to the Grand Trunk Pacific: 'You have $10,000,000 on hand, pay us back the money we put into the construction of the road,' and the government has to aid to that extent, the only reason the government has to pay is because the Grand Trunk Railway, instead of paying for its own rolling stock, chooses to advance the money to the Grand Trunk Pacific to supply rolling stock for their use.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that is possible.

I desire information concerning the estimates that were made when this project was proposed to the House on August 11, 1903. At that time, Mr. Blair was Minister of Railways and Canals, and. in placing his statement before the House, he estimated that the direct and indirect liability of this country on account of thi3 project would be $139,000,000. We have had various estimates as to the cost of the work within the last two or three days during which this matter has been under discussion. The estimate has now reached, I think, in the neighbourhood of $250,000,000, an amount greatly in excess of the estimate of Mr. Blair as "Minister of Railways and Canals, and he was looked upon by the government at that time as very extravagant. I assume that the government has looked over the estimates which were given at that time on which Mr. Blair based his conclusion that the cost would be ,$139,000,-

000. May I ask if these statements have been* gone over by the present Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) or by the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) or by any person appointed to represent the government? For, it is important to know upon what data the present estimates are based.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These things may be interesting in themselves and proper subjects of discussion, but I Cannot see that they have any bearing on this loan. Therefore, I have not given attention to the matter referred to. I am aware that the Minister of Railway^ and Canals (Mr. Graham) recently gave the House the best information he could as to the probable cost of the road. I know that the estimate is very much greater than we ever anticipated, and to that extent it is a matter of regret, but there seems to be no help for it. If the cost of the eastern division, as it is called, which has very often been spoken of, had been much greater than our anticipations and every other railway whose cost was estimated at the same time had been constructed -without increased expense, I should have begun to feel that, perhaps, there was some room for criticism of the government or their commissioners as to the cost of the eastern division. But, when we find that railways everywhere are costing more than the estimates made at that time, when we find that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, with all the experience and skill at their command-for they have the benefit of the experience and skill of the engineering staff of the Grand Trunk-is obliged to pay so much more than the estimate for their part of the road, we can look more charitably upon the results of the efforts of the commissioners who are charged with the duty of directing the con [DOT] struction of _ this eastern division. These are interesting and important questions, but I think that the answer given by. the Minister of Railways and Canals on a recent day covers prettv much the question of my hon. friend (Mr. Blain). At all events, I do not see that this has a very important bearing upon the question o'f this loan. It is a question of loaning the company so much money, as a banker would loan it; and whatever the cost of the road, be it large or small, it is not affected by this except for the explanation that it is because of the increased cost of the road that the company is obliged to come and ask for the loan.

Would there be any objection on the part of the government to laying upon the table estimates upon which Mr. Blair at that time based his statement of the cost of the proposed railway? I have the right to assume that, as he was Minister of Railways and Canals at that
.Mr. BLAIN.
time, and giving to the House and the country the estimated cost of the construction of this important national highway, he would only speak after having had estimates on which to base his statement. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) may say that it has .no bearing upon the proposed loan and that it is important to * separate one from the other. But we have the right to criticise the government in this matter. They drove out a gentleman from the government because he was extravagant and his estimate was largely in excess of what other ministers led the the country to believe the road would cost. Surely we have the right now, even though the Minister of Finance may venture to say it is not apropos, to ask that he. lay on the table at some future day the estimates on which Mr. Blair, then Minister of Railways and Canals, based his statement of the cost of the road, that statement being the direct and indirect liability of the country would be $139,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have to leave my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to deal with that. I do not know whether Mr. Blair had estimates of an official character; I could not say the source of his information. If there are official estimates that were made by the department at that time, I imagine that my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) would have the right to have them brought down. I do not know, and I will have to leave it to the Minister of Railways.

I think that the matter brought forward by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) is not only strictly in order, but that it is most pertinent in view of that which is before us. Referring to the schedule of this Bill, page 6, paragraph 2, I find the following:
And whereas owing to the high standard of the railway being constructed by the Pacific Company, as well as the increased cost of labour, material and supplies, the cost of completing the construction of the prairie section will considerably exceed that estimated.
Now, I do not think that we should lightly say that the increased cost over the estimate has nothing to do with this case, which is the excuse the Minister of Finance puts forth. Like the preamble of any other document, this is the part which is to be used for the most particular manner of construction that can be applied to the document as a whole. It is stated that the people of Canada are making this loan solely because there has been a mistake in the estimated cost of the prairie section. Surely, we ought to know how that mistake arose, whose fault it was, whether we were deceived by the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific, or how it hap-

pened, and what we had better do about it. All that information is most pertinent, and I do think we ought to have the very best light possible thrown upon the subject in view of the fact that we are basing a contract on this preamble.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Referring to the previous section, mention is made of the mortgage to guarantee certain advances by the Grand Trunk. An estimate was prepared by the Grand Trunk people in respect of these bonds that they were to guarantee. The mortgage sets forth the facts of the case in a manner the hon. gentleman will appreciate.

But the hon. minister will not say, as representing the country, that he is going to take the estimates of the other party, the party with whom he is supposed to deal at arm's-length. Mr. Blair had to resign because he did not think the country would stand for a transaction of that kind, and his remaining colleagues thought that his estimate was too great. There must surely, then, have been some, estimate made on behalf of the people. Surely the Minister of Finance would have to have an estimate from his own standpoint to see whether he is being misled or deceived. This loan is necessary because the cost will considerably exceed the estimate, but surely that estimate must have been made on behalf of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily on behalf of the government; the government has no direct concern with that. The Grand Trunk were guaranteeing the moneys required for the completion of the enterprise, and we were concerned in having the mortgage express that estimate correctly. It was their estimate, and I do not think it is of very much importance to us whether it was a correct estimate or not. What we are concerned about is that if we are going to pay one dollar out of any fund contributed by the government of Canada, or by guarantee of the government of Canada, or by loan of the government of Canada, we must see that the money is paid out on evidence of bona fide cost. The question of estimates is not by any means as important as my hon. friend argues.

The country was guaranteeing 75 per cent of the cost. We have two deals with these people, and we are asked to give $10,000,000 more to them. We are asked to do that by a document drawn up by the government because there was a mistake in the estimate, or an error; at any rate, the estimate was not correct. Surely we are concerned in that. If the country was guaranteeing 75 per cent of it, then it was of importance to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This estimate has reference to the balance, not to the 75 per cent.
The words are: 'Whereas the cost of the prairie section will exceed that estimate'.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the mortgage was being prepared the Grand Trunk people knew they had to guarantee whatever the balance might be, and they made an estimate for themselves and for their investors. It was not our guarantee, it was not our money; it was to be their guarantee.
You had to 'act on it.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They had to raise that money themselves, and they found it necessary to express in their first mortgage, what amount they would assign to Ithe prairie section. They made an estimate, and they assigned a certain proportion of that mortgage fund to the prairie section. Now it turns out (that it was not enough.
I do not think we are very much concerned as to whether a mistake was made there or not. It was not made with any funds of the government; it was made as respects the Grand Trunk share of the obligation.

You must take some cognizance of the estimate that was made, for it, is plain to the committee that if the proper estimate had been made the company would not now be here asking for a loan of $10,000,000. That is clearly of importance to us and the minister cannot cast it aside in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is quite clear that the estimate, while it may have been proper at the moment, according to the information they had, has turned out to be an insufficient estimate; that owing, as they allege, to the increased cost of material and various other causes, the money is not. enough, and they want more. But that does not necessarily prove that the estimate was an improper one. It was an estimate in which they had no interest to mislead, it was an estimate of what they themselves have to provide for their share of the obligation, and they made it with the best information they had, I have no doubt, made it all in good faith, made it intelligently. But it proves to be not sufficient; that is all.

Supposing the estimate given by this company to-day turns out to be equally incorrect. How do we know that the estimate they make to-day is a correct estimate, and that next session we will not be asked for $10,000,000 more, and the session after foT $30,000,000 more?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know the future. If I believed this $10,000,000 was

not enough, in all probability I would be asking the House to make it $11,000,000 or $12,000,000. But I accept the assurance of our engineers that it is probably enough, and I believe it will be enough.

We are to-day being asked to finance them again to the extent of $10,000,000. What we did then is the only excuse for us now to pay out $10,000 -000 more.
loan $10,000,000, and we want you to make us a mortgage which is a guarantee, so far as a mortgage can be a guarantee.'
This eminent legal authority did not imagine what I have just read; some officer or some minister gave him these facts to put in that document.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The document carries the estimate on its face.
Mr. FIELDING, what they did.
Not what we did, but
It shows the company's estimate was wrong.
Didn't we do any thing?	J

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in that transaction.

We made a transaction in regard to building a National Transcontinental Railway; and it is not what we did, it is what they did not do that makes the trouble. Before this clause passes the committee I would like to enter my protest against any further loan of the people's money for the building of a road that, while it is called a great transcontinental system, is not and cannot be, under this legislation, the property of the people. A great national undertaking ought to be controlled by the nation, especially when the nation supplies the money and credit for the construction of the road. Government ownership can never be realized in connection with this great national undertaking. It has not been in the past and it will not be in this case. It has not been in regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway. The German empire to-day is dominating the world because it has nationalized its railways. We have been told in this House and our delegates to Great Britain have told the people of the empire that the great contribution that Canada has made to the empire has been the building of a transcontinental railway, which makes an intercontinental railway between Europe and Asia. That may be so as a statement, but, as a fact, this road is not owned or controlled by the nation, is not built from
a national standpoint, but is built by a private corporation in such a way that the control of the National Transcontinental Railway may, any day, pass into the hands of those hostile to this country. One can imagine at the very crisis of the empire that it might be disclosed that this Grand Trunk Pacific system is owned and controlled by German capital, and so manipulated for years ahead that the system would absolutely fall down, and, as far as being a factor in or a portion of the imperial defence is concerned, so many points of weakness would develop that the road would not be of any use from an imperial or business point of view. Any day this so-called transcontinental railway, built by the money of this nation, may be owned by a foreign corporation, who might use it to the detriment of the country and of the empire. Any day it is possible that Mr. Jas. J. Hill, who has a rival transcontinental system in the United States, or a still greater magnate in the railway world, Mr. Harriman, may secure the absolute control of this so-called transcontinental railway system which the people have built so far and which they must see through. We are bound to see this road through, and we are bound to see it through as a nation. If we do see it through as a nation, why should not the nation control it? The United States to-day are building the Panama canal, but they are building it themselves as a state proposition. It is a national undertaking and it is even being constructed by engineers in the service of the state. There is no contractor in that case. They are moving on the lines of nationalism and they are making the Panama canal, which is a great transcontinental proposition, the property of the state. We are building a great system, but we are allowing it to pass into the possession of a private company, whose stock is kicked about in the money market of the world. A great mistake has been made and this mistake ought now to be corrected. The opportunity has presented itself at this crisis to recover the control of this Transcontinental Railway and to make it a great national asset, as it ought to be for the benefit of the country and of the empire. We have had experience of great transcontinental railways being in the hands of private corporations, and I am prepared to assert here to-day and prove that the Canadian Pacific Railway, which was largely subsidized by this nation, which was said to be a national proposition, is administered absolutely in the interest of the shareholders and of the men who have the control of that railway, and without any regard for the nation. The Grand Trunk will be exactly of the same kind. I am further prepared to assert that as a matter

of fact the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific railways treat the people of the United States better, in the way of passenger and freight rates, than they treat the people of Canada. This has been going on year after year. Yet, in spite of that fact, in spite of the way things are moving in the world, in spite of the fact that the essential theory of nationality is to control all the national highways, we are continuing to build these railways and to find the money without having the control of them. There is no way we can have the control of them, to use them for the benefit of the nation, and to make them a great government proposition.
Of course we will be told that the Canadian people are such an inferior lot that they are not able to administer and construct and own a great national highway, but I do not subscribe to any such doctrine as that. I have every confidence in my fellow countrymen that they are quite competent to undertake such a project and that all they want is the opportunity to do it. I believe that the people of this country want to see the Intercolonial Railway developed as a national enterprise by taking it absolutely out of politics and by running it for the benefit of the nation and not of a party. I believe that the people of this country are competent not only to construct and operate profitably a line between the provinces, but a great national highway across the Dominion. And, Sir, within the next five years, within the next ten years, the whole energy and resources of the Canadian people, I venture to predict, will be devoted to securing the control of the great national highways of the country. Public feeling is running in that direction, public feeling is antagonistic to the legislation we are passing here to-day in relation to the Grand Trunk Pacific, public feeling is in favour of recovering the ground we have lost. I have- no hesitation in saying that the movement in favour of the nationalization of our railways will continue to grow, and that before the next election it will become the real issue before the people. It would have been the easiest possible thing for this government to have obtained in the London market the control of the common shares of the Grand Trunk which control the Grand Trunk Railway system and now are to control the National Transcontinental Railway. These shares have been kicked about in the London market, they can be obtained for a comparatively small sum of money and they should be taken possession of by the government. The only way we can retrieve the blunder we are making today; the only way we can recover this National Transcontinental Railway for the people and make it truly national will be to buy the controlling shares of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the London money market. I believe at this stage of the Mr W. F. MACLEAN.
proceedings the people of Canada would indorse any proposition of the government which would tend towards securing the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The Grand Trunk Railway, the Grand Trank Pacific, and the Intercolonial Railway together would have been a great national system. Their amalgamation under national control would have been of immense service to the country, and while the system would be a rival to the Canadian Pacific Railway, its benefit in that respect would not be so great as in the fact that it would widen and broaden out the railroad service of this country and provide transportation facilities where further facilities are badly needed. There is an unnecessary duplication of railways in this country, and the solution of the railway problem is not the building of one line alongside of another so much as the broadening out of the service and the extension of it where it is most needed. My protest may be in vain; many a protest made by me in this House has apparently been in vain, but I will try to retain my seat in the House so as to be here on the day when the mandate of the people of Canada will go from this parliament insisting on the nationalization of our railway systems, and insisting that this great railway which we are to-day building with the money of the people and giving to a private company shall be restored to its rightful owners. We know that this National Transcontinental Railway may be controlled by outsiders, may be controlled by rival railroads in the United States, may even be controlled by capitalistic interests that are hostile to Canada and hostile to the empire. And, when the right hon. the Prime Minister goes to England again and tells them that Canada is doing something for the empire in the building of a Transcontinental Railway system, I hope he will be able to say that he has regained control of it for Canada and for the empire. I reiterate my protest against any further giving of the credit of this country to build and complete a system that will be owned by private corporations. The people of Canada came to the aid of the Canadian Pacific Railway because of the vicissitudes of that company, and they will have to come to the aid of this National Transcontinental Railway because of its vicissitudes, but we should take advantage of the opportunity to recover control of that road and make it a great national system. You may rest assured that if we do not do so now we will have to do it some day, and all the agitation which is bound to ensue towards that end could have been avoided if we had had the wisdom to nationalize this railroad in the beginning. I conclude by protesting against granting any more of the money of the country for a proposition of this kind which does not lead to the nationalization of that railway.

The question of the exact position of this guarantee which was alluded to again this afternoon is very important. There is no doubt in my mind that the rentals of the leased lines come in ahead of this guarantee because they are classed as working expenses according to an answer of the Finance Minister. But a question has arisen also as to whether this guarantee comes ahead of the first preference stock, for instance. From the answer to the question which I asked some days ago, I see that Mr. Shep-ley takes decided ground that this guarantee does come ahead of the preference stock, so I suppose we are bound to accept that statement although I would call the attention of the House to the fact that this preference stock was originally bonds and the bonds were changed by this House from the status of bonds to stock, and that in the Act providing for this preference stock it is stated that they are entitled to certain specific dividends. The word ' entitled ' is a pretty strong word and when you say a stock is entitled to a specific dividend it seems to me to be a question whether there is not some charge on the road in connection with it, although Mr. Shepley takes strong ground that this guarantee comes ahead of even the first preference stock.
I want to call the minister's attention

to another case in order to show how much more careful some peonle are to guard the interests of bond holders than he has been in this instance with regard to the money of the people. In 35 Victoria, Chapter 64, there is an Act concerning the Grand Trunk Railway and the Montreal and Champlain Railroad Company. In that Act there is a guarantee of bonds much the same as this guarantee of bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Section 5 of that Act provides that the Grand Trunk Railway guarantees the payment of the interest and the principal of these bonds. Then it goes on to say that the interest shall form part of the working expenses of the Grand Trunk Railway as defined in the Grand Trunk Railway Arrangements Act. In other words the interest on the bonds of the Montreal and Champlain Railroad Company, which were guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway, formed part of the working expenses of the Grand Trunk, which, under the Grand Trunk Railway Arrangements Act, as is the case in every other railway, are a first charge on the receipts of the road. Why was not the government as careful in this instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are prior bonds in this case, and anything we would do by way of creating a lien ahead of these bonds would certainly be a breach of faith, which my hon. friend would not' ask us to commit. If there were no bonds outstanding, we could make any conditions apply we chose respecting a new issue, but you cannot make exceptional conditions apply to a new issue to the disadvantage of outstanding securities.

I am not advocating that in this instance, but I call attention to the fact that there is a case in which the responsibility of the Grand Trunk Railway for interest is made a first lien on its traffic receipts, and there may be lots of other cases. The question is where the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway, in this instance, comes in reference to their stocks and bonds, &c. speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
