I am sure that my hon. friend will believe me when I say that the object of this government, as has been outlined in its policy, has always been the development of our own national ports This object has been attained as far as possible in the recent French treaty. One of the objects of the building of this transcontinental railway was to give us an all Canadian line which would lead to the development of our Canadian ports on the Atlantic seaboard. It must be borne in mind at the present juncture, however, that every dollar or every cent we j,dd to the rate of freight on the products of the west will reduce the price of those products to the producer. The object of building a high class road all the way through to our own ports was" to get the minimum of rate freights. If the situation were just as my hon. friend has outlined it his conclusion would be correct, but, unfortunately, the comparison made between the proposed Grand Trunk Pacific line and the Intercolonial Railway cannot be borne out. Not having an engineer's knowledge of this line I would have made the same error that my hon. friend has made. Of the three steep grades I mentioned on the Intercolonial Railway, two are west of Moncton, and there is one each way on the Transcontinental Railway. Consequently, it might be assumed that the same load could be drawn over each. But, when you come to work it out practically that is not the result at all. The fundamental principle is that the ruling grade controls the load. A pusher grade does not interfere with the load at all because you use a second engine to get over that grade, and the load which can be carried is limited only by the ruling grade. The ruling grade on the Grand Trunk Pacific to Moncton is 4:10 of one per cent and a train load can be carried up to the capacity of a 4:10 of one per cent grade. The pusher obviates the difficulty which would otherwise be experienced in getting over the steep grade
in one place. On the Intercolonial Railway, although only three grades were mentioned of a steep character the standard is a one per cent grade east and west all over and no train load can be carried that exceeds the capacity of the ruling grade which just makes the carrying capacity of the Intercolonial Railway practically one half the carrying capacity of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

Has the minister any data to show how many individual grades there are on the Intercolonial Railway of [DOT]one per cent or over? I will go further. How many grades are there on the Intercolonial Railway of 4-10ths of one per cent and over?

speechtext: I have a copy of the profile of the Intercolonial Railway.Tasked my chief engineer to-day to give me something along that line and he tells me the grades are practically so common east and . west that the standard or the ruling grade of the Intercolonial Railway is one per cent, and we cannot load our trains to any higher capacity than one per cent. I have had a little calculation made to show that, as a matter of fact, from Montreal east the train loads on the Intercolonial Railway would practically be only one-half as great as the train loads that could be carried over the Grand Trunk Pacific. That would be a serious disadvantage. It would mean possibly, even if we made the best arrangement we could, that the freight rate would be considerably higher over that portion of the line at least than it would be on a road with a ruling grade of 4-10ths of one per cent, because the cost would nearly double in the carrying. House in Committee on Bill (No. 34) to incorporate the Ontario and Michigan Power Company.-Mr. Conmee.
On section 1,

Notice has been given of a number of amendments. It is proposed to strike out sections 2 and 13, also 15, and 'to substitute other sections. The notice given by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce), which denied powers of expropriation so far as the Nipigon river is concerned, has been accepted and embodied in the amendments. As we discuss the Bill, section by section, it will be seen that the amendments have met, I think fairly, all the objections that were raised the -other evening when the Bill was under discussion.

I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by certain sections being struck out and others substituted and certain matters being agreed to. I would be glad if the hon. gentleman would make it clear to us at this stage just what is proposed.

The first amendment is that section 2 of the Bill be struck out. Section 2 provided for the declaration that the works were for the general advantage of Canada. In order to satisfy my hon. friend it is proposed to strike that out.

In order to make it clear that the company will not be permitted to export power from Canada except subject to the Electricity Inspection Act and the Electricity Exportation Act, 1907, this clause is inserted in place of sections 13 and 15:
The provisions of the Electricity Inspection Act, 1907, and of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act shall apply to the company and its undertakings.
2. The company shall not export any electrical power until it has obtained a license to do so under section 4 of the last mentioned Act, and such license may provide that the quantity of power to be exported shall be limited to the surplus after the company has supplied for distribution to consumers for use in Canada power to the extent defined by such license at prices and in accordance with conditions, rules and regulations, prescribed by the Governor in Council.
Speaking generally that clause is practically a copy of section 4 of the Electricity Exportation Act embodied in the Bill. Section 5 of section 19 is to be struck out and the following substituted for it.
The expropriation powers hereby conferred upon the company shall not ibe exercised by it until the plans mentioned in section 18 of this Act shall have received the approval therein ^provided for; and with respect to any lands upon the Nipigon river shall not be exercised, except as to such lands as may be required for the purposes of its transmission lines.
That cuts out entirely the powers of expropriation in regard to any water-power upon the Nipigon river and confines it under other sections of the Bill entirely to the Pigeon river, which is the purport of the notice of motion given by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce). I may say that in section 18 the word * Nipigon ' will have to be struck out. Then there is a clause that was agreed upon and does not affect the powers of the company, but is merely for the protection
Will the hon. member explain what he means by 'agreed upon'? -agreed upon, in what way?

Agreed upon between the promoters of this BUI and the Arrow river people,-but I will read the clause:
The said expropriation powers shall not be exercised as to any dams for the storage of water now constructed or that may hereafter be constructed by the Arrow River Tributary Slide and Boom Company.
This company is a lumbering concern with certain dams for storage areas on tributaries of the Pigeon river, but not on the Pigeon river. Under the Bill of last year introduced in the Senate, this company was asking for powers for the storage of water, that is, they were asking to go out, upon the tributaries of the rivers and create storage for power purposes, and, in
that way, their interest would clash with that of this lumbering company. That, clause was agreed upon last year between the representatives of the lumbering company and this company. Therefore, I desire to have that clause stand. I might, for a moment, call the attention of the committee to the provision of section 14 of the Bill.
I think that hon. gentlemen will find that goes a good deal farther in public protection than any legislation heretofore passed by this House has gone. It first provides that the rates to be charged to consumers should be fixed from time to time by the Railway Commissioners of Canada. When the Bill was under discussion before the committee last time, an hon. member, Mr. Fowke, said he had two objections to it. One was that he was not in favour of permitting the company to export any portion of the power from the Canadian side without control. He was not satisfied with the provisions under section 15 as it then stood in the Bill, which, I pointed out, was put there for the purpose of giving that protection. But he had another objection,-and he was not speaking particularly against this Bill, he was announcing a principle. He was opposed to a perpetual franchise. I think that this section 14 does not give a perpetual franchise, it gives the company only a limited opportunity, under restrictions., to utilize a natural resource. If the idea of a lease, if that was advanced by the hon. member, were to prevail, what would be the result? Let me take the water-power regulations of the Ontario government. They provide for a twenty-year lease in dealing with a water-power. I have one of the leases here, and can send it to the hon. gentleman if he wishes to see it. It provides for a lease of twenty years and a renewal after twenty years, the rental to be paid may be increased, or the rates to consumers reduced, and if they cannot agree with the company on these points they may arbitrate.

Is the government absolutely bound to renew the lease at the ; end of the twenty-year period, or may it ' exercise its judgment as to that?
:	Mr. CONMEE. The government is bound
to renew the lease at the end of the twenty-[DOT] year period, subject to the conditions I i have named, or to expropriate the property,

paying the company under arbitration if they cannot agree upon the price.
Is the value of the franchise excluded?

I cannot answer that question, I do not know the exact regulations as they stand to-day ; I -speak of them as they appear in a lease which I have, the regulations as I knew them a few years ago. If my information is correct, the present government does not agree to arbitrate as to the value of the property, but only as to the rental to be given to the government as to the rates they may charge the consumer. They take the power under their commission, the Hydro-Electric Commission, to regulate the rates. Section 14 provides much better protection. Twenty years is a long time. This does not limit it to twenty years, or ten, or five years. It provides that rates may be fixed ' from time to time.' Any consumer may make application, and the rates may he reduced. But it goes much further than that. It provides that the board shall regulate the conditions of the service. What does that mean? It means the hours of service, the facilities that shall be given to the consumer to utilize the power, the delivery of the power not at a station, and then to be stepped down by the community that wants to use it, but the delivery, if the board so orders, to the premises of the consumer, the board having full control over all the circumstances. There is no kind of dispute, I submit, that can well arise between the consumer and the company that the board will not have absolute control over and power to regulate from time to time. I do not know that any better protection for the public interest could be worked out. I submit also that this Bill and this company, like all others, are subject to the general law of the country. If, in the future, it is the policy of this government, or of any future government, to pass a general law regulating the use of water-power, making conditions by which it will be taken from the company, the power exists to do it, that is, general legislation would do it. But there is special power under our constitution which gives us this right. These works can, at any time, either before or after their construction, be declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada, and the government can impose any conditions they please. They can take over the works on any method that may to them seem fair and satisfactory. So, I submit, this' Bill h^s gone a long way to settle what is a pretty intricate question as to the best conditions for the protection of the public interest. I think it goes much further than previous legislation.
Then, if hon. members will examine the Bill, they will see that municipal interests

are protected. First, the company cannot enter within the limits of any municipality without the consent of that municipality, and not its consent merely but its consent expressed by by-law. What section is that?

I have not the Bill before me, but I think it is section II. It goes further as to cities and towns, which are, perhaps, more important. The company cannot enter a city or town, cannot have any rights there, until a by-law is carried, not by the corporation, but by the qualified electors, that is, those entitled to vote on money by-laws. I do not know what possible conditions could be drawn to better safeguard the public interest in this respect than these clauses of the Bill. If hon. gentlemen will glance them over, I am satisfied that they will say that they go about as far as they ought to go. I may say that I have more at stake, as a representative, in this Bill than any other hon. member. I represent the community that is most deeply interested in the Bill. If the Bill is not what I can, as such -representative, iustify before the community, I shall be damaged, no doubt.

to be dealt with entirely by the Ontario legislature.

There is another reason why this Bill should be delayed. It affects very materially the policy of the provincial government. That government believes that it is entitled to use these water-powers foT the purposes of revenue if necessary. Some of them at least they are renting at an annual rental, and such leases are renewable, subject to the provision that the rentals may be increased if necessary from time to time. I apprehend that the Ontario government has not been notified of these proposed changes, nor have we heard from it. Probably it would be as much opposed to the Bill in its present form a? in its original shape, because it thinks that it has a right to control these water-powers. For that reason, if for no other, the Bill ought to be delayed. As regards the nature of the changes, we have only just received them and have not had time to consider them carefully. The hon. gentleman has put forward a strange doctrine on the _ question of the right of this Dominion to control a stream. This government has the right to control navigable streams, but I put a question to the hon. gentleman in that connection to this effect: Suppose some 20 or 25 miles of a stream are navigable, say at its mouth, and all the rest of the way, some 400 miles, it is not navigable; does he contend that because a small portion is navigable, the whole stream is under the federal authority? I think he said it is. That is about the situation in the case of the Nipi gon river. Only a small portion of that river is navigable, and for that reason my hon. friend contends that the Dominion parliament has the right to control tha stream throughout its whole length. But the provincial government thinks differently, and there is a good deal of reason in its contention.
This Bill, as amended does not give the company anv rights on the Nipigon at all.

I was speaking of my hon. friend's contention and applying it to that stream, which is one of the streams in question. There are many changes in this Bill, and we have not time to consider them, and it would not be possible to understand them at this sitting. He had better allow the Bill to stand over until we hear fiom the Ontario government.
If we cannot legislate without the consent of the Ontario government, we will not be able to legislate on a great many subjects.
If we legislate with regard to provincial interests?

Are we to have no opinions of our own? There can be no provincial question as regards the Pigeon river, because it is a boundary stream, and the land passed out of the possession of the Crown more than 50 years ago, so that there can possibly be no provincial interests in that river.
Perhaps if the hon. gentleman was representing the province of Ontario he would think differently.

I shall not debate that question with my hon. friend. But the proposition that this Bill should stand over until we can learn the views of the Ontario government is one to which I cannot consent. I do not want to unduly press the Bill, but of course if hon. gentlemen choose to take a hostile course, we cannot accomplish very much just now, as the hour for private Bills is nearly up. But I do not see what good purpose will be served by putting it off. The Bill should be dealt with on its merits. If the majority of the House are opposed to it and will vote that way, the Bill will fall to the ground.
Mr;. LENNOX. As regards what the hon. gentleman said about our being opposed to this Bill, I hope he does not take that view of the matter. When it was called a little after eight o'clock, I asked him to explain, and he gave a very elaborate explanation which has taken up most of the time down to this moment. We certainly have no time to consider it now. If he prefers that we should discuss it for the quarter of an hour left within which it can be discussed, we shall do so, but we cannot dispose of the Bill to-night and he might just as well move that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are some amendments to which there can be no possible objections. For instance the amendment striking out clause 2, which clause was objected to and is now removed. Surely that can be passed.

But we do not know how far we may be dealing with provincial rights until we get through. We might commit ourselves to some legislation by passing clauses which we would not pass in the light of what may come afterwards. What strikes me is that we are straining here to find excuses for doing what we ought to do only if we were in the Ontario legislature. I cannot see how we can gain anything by attempting to do that. We have enough business of our own to attend to federally in regard to matters that appertain to the Dominion without bothering to be a court of appeal or advisory board to any provincial government.
I have not taken any part in the discussion so far, but I have listened every time this Bill has been discussed. My hon.

friend is not lacking in astuteness or knowledge of legislative procedure and, although not a lawyer, he is just as well able as lots of lawyers to discuss this matter even from a legal standpoint. I am sorry he has not told us of some reason why the Ontario legislature cannot do all that he wants done and provide all the safeguards he says he is now willing to provide in this Bill. Why can they not provide them? Why not allow the legislature of Ontario to deal with provincial matters ? We are not competent to deal with matters that appertain solely to the people of Ontario and we are not the judges of what they should do. They are the sole judges. We have no right to think that we can do as well as they can and we are not insulting ourselves if we say we cannot do as well as they can in regard to provincial matters. I do not doubt that a good many of us would vote one way on this Bill in this parliament and an entirely different way upon a similar Bill if we were in the provincial legislature. What troubles me is that we are dealing with this matter as a federal matter without being sure that there is any need whatever for federal legislation. We have no right to exercise jurisdiction here unless the province cannot deal with the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the argument which he has presented does not apply. We do not commit ourselves to the Bill until the preamble is accepted. Until that is done there is nothing done. There are some provisions in the Bill to which he took exception and which are to be eliminated by my hon. friend from Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee). To this certainly he cannot object. This Bill, as it is amended by my hon. friend, contains nothing as to which there should be any debate except as to the power of expropriation. My hon. friend has eliminated from the Bill that part which deals with the Nipigon river as to which I was against him. Now, the powers of expropriation are confined to a river which is international. There is a good deal to be said against the proposition of my hon. friend from Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster? that the powers there are vested in the province of Ontario, and there is a good deal to be said in favour of the other proposition that the powers are vested here. That is a question which can be discussed at the proper time, but, it seems to me we would be advancing the work for which we are here if we accepted this cart of the Bill and reserved the discussion for the part which is really contentious.

My reason in suggesting what I did was partially the statement of the hon. gentleman himself that the Bill, as it was proposed to be amended, he felt quite satisfied, would not be objectionable to the Ontario government if they were consulted.
I did not make that statement.

That was the impression I had from the language he used. I thought, therefore, if it was submitted to them and we had information to that effect from them it would very much simplify it here and that while we might still think that they had acted unwisely, if they did not desire to exercise control over these water-powers, there are some members of this House who would not oppose the Bill very strongly. My own opinion is that these water-powers belong to the provinces. They are the assets of the province and they should be used as such. They are at the present time renting them from year to year and getting a very considerable income from some of them. They have announced to the world that their policy is to take the whole of them under their control and to develop them on provincial lines. Since what they have done has inured to their benefit, they using their own property and making money out of it, why should we take to ourselves the right to expropriate, or rather to deprive them of a part of the property that belongs to them? It is taking from them a right which they possess. I do not think we should do it.

The notice regarding these amendments states that they will be proposed on Monday next. I suppose they were put in too late to take effect to-day. Therefore, my hon. friend from West Al-goma (Mr. Boyce) is perfectly justified in considering that these amendments should be taken on Monday. Instead of continuing the debate it would be much better to defer the consideration of the matter until Monday.
I gave the notice for 'Friday.5
The hon. gentleman must have been too late to give the notice for this evening, because the notice says 'Monday.'

This discussion, I submit, is irregular. The Bill should be taken up clause by clause and discussed, whereas the committee has been allowed to discuss it generally. The notice of my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) is practically the same as this notice, so that there has been lots of time as far as the notice is concerned. Let me say a word in answer to the hon. member who spoke a few minutes ago (Mr. Lancaster) and who desired to know my reason why this parliament has been asked to pass this legislation instead of the provincial legislature. All I can say is that I thought I did give in the discus-

si on of that question when the Bill was up for its second reading and again in committee, the very best reasons. I gave the judgment of the Privy Council that this parliament and this parliament alone should create this company.
To do what?
To carry out the undertaking which this company is asking to be allowed to carry out.
Did that court have this Bill before-it? It depends on what you put in your Bill.
If my hon. friend is going to make a Bill for these promoters, or if he is going to dictate to them what they shall put in their Bill, I do not know where he will land them.

No, I am not going to do that. But no court can ahead of time, say that a certain Bill which is afterwards brought in to parliament is a Bill that can only be passed by the Dominion. If you put a stated case to them, the answer to which you must know will be in the affirmative, saying that the Dominion can do this or that you can get that answer from the court, but the court could not say that a Bill to be introduced by my hon. friend at a later date is a Bill which this parliament can alone pass.
The best authority we have in this land has said so. The courts have decided that point.
What have they decided?

I could give my hon. friend no less an authority than that of Sir Oliver Mowat. I was brought up in the school of provincial Tights in which Sir Oliver was the teacher. I am still sound on that question. Here is the language of that gentleman dealing with a Bill intros duced under similar circumstances:
The only authority conferred upon a provincial legislature to incorporate companies is for the incorporation of companies with provincial objects. The undersigned construes this authority to mean objects provincial as to the province creating the company.
Then he goes on to give cases in which the courts held a similar view, and he uses this language:
It would seem to follow that the statute in question which confers upon the company authority to acquire, cultivate, improve, and sell land Dot only in the province of Nova ocotra but also in the province of New Brunswick and elsewhere, is not limited to provincial objects in the sense in which that expression is used in the British North America Act, and therefore the enactment is ultra vires.
That is not this case.

No, but it is a case which is similar. He then commends Sir John Thomson's rulings with regard to a Quebec case in which Sir John Thompson recommended disallowance because the company undertook to divert a navigable stream, and Sir Oliver himself applied this tuling to tiie case of the Kaministiquia river for the same reasons. We have also had the opinion of the Minister of Justice given on the floor of the House that this parliament can alone confer the power which this company asks.

I am afraid I will have to withdraw the compliment I paid my hon. friend on his legal attainment; it was paid out of politeness and I regret to have to take it back. Everybody knows that when a company operates in different provinces it is not a provincial work, but this company is going to, as I understand, is going to operate entirely within Ontario.
The trouble is that you don't understand it.

The decision given by the learned and much respected authority quoted by the hon gentleman is based upon the ground that the company referred to in that case was going to operate in two different provinces, and not being confined to the one province it was of course a work for the general advantage of Canada.
Does not the hon. gentleman see in this Bill that the company is not confined to one province?
That is not the effect of this Bill.
The company operates not only in Ontario but in the United States.
You might say it would operate in Mexico or Australia, but that does not help you.

When this Bill was first introduced it was considered of such importance by the Ontario government that they sent a special counsel to object to it in committee. The hon. gentleman since that time has made many changes in his Bill, and the Ontario government should certainly have an opportunity of considering these changes. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) is rather hostile to the Ontario government, but that is his right and privilege.

The hon. gentleman should not impute motives to me. I am not unduly hostile to the Ontario government; I have no personal quarrel with them.
xtPRIL 30, 1909

But the hon. gentleman refuses to wait until the Ontario government is consulted. In my opinion the Ontario government is just as anxious to develop the water-powers of that province as this parliament can be, and if the hon. gentleman has a proper project to submit to them he will no doubt receive their cooperation.

Nine o'clock.
The hour for private Bills expired.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed in Committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 128) to authorize a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: At six o'clock I was trying to correct a wrong impression which seemed to prevail as to a comparison of the grades on the Transcontinental and on the Intercolonial Railway from Levis to Moncton. The leader of the opposition suggested that an arrangement might be made by which grain from Midland could be carried to the sea board by the Grand Trunk and the Intercolonial Railway. From the Intercolonial Railway standpoint I would approve of that provided no injury were done to the shippers. But, the hon. gentleman also suggested that we might do that even if the Intercolonial Railway carried the grain for the present at a loss, and as head of the Railway Department I must dissent from that proposition. I think the Intercolonial Railway as a government road should be treated in the same way as other roads. If the government came to the conclusion that the Intercolonial Railway should carry the grain at a loss then it would be the duty of parliament, after ascertaining what that loss was, to pass a special vote to compensate the Intercolonial Railway and not charge it with the whole burden. In Australia, if the government asks the government railway to carry goods at a nonpaying rate then the government passes an appropriation to compensate the railway, and under similar circumstances, a like provision should be made in Canada. I have not been able to consult with any per-so so as to get accurate information on the point, but my opinion is that the grade on the Intercolonial from Montreal to Moncton is no higher than the ruling grade on the Grand Trunk Railway from Midland to Montreal.
No higher?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: My own impression i that they are about on an equal footing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not yet dealt with the real difficult which I raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The right hon. the Prime Minister was about to speak.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The difficulty suggested by my hon. friend, if I understood him aright, is as to what will become of the traffic between the west and the east during the interval which must elapse before the bridge at Quebec is completed. I need not say that the accident which has befallen the bridge is a very serious interference with the contract. We had expected when we entered into the contract that the bridge, which had been in progress for some time, ivould be completed about the same time as the road itself, and but for the unfortunate event which has taken place our calculations, I think, would have come out about right. The bridge has been down now for eighteen months and the plans for the reconstruction will not be ready for some time, probably not before the end of the year. I believe the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) was about right when he said that on the most favourable estimate the bridge could not be completed ready for traffic before 1915. After the lesson which we have received, after having plans prepared by engineers whom we had reason to believe were the most competent engineers on the continent, and whose efforts have proved so fatal, we have felt it necessary to take every possible precaution. We have confided the preparation of the plans for the new bridge to a board composed of the most eminent engineers to be found in Europe and on this continent. They are proceeding with the work but I do not know yet when the plans will be prepared, perhaps they will take the best part of the year. In the meantime how are 'we to connect the two branches of the railway, the sections from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton? I will not surprise the House by saying that the Minister of Railways and myself and the cabinet have given some attention to that question. We thought that perhaps it would be possible to place a ferry on the river. I am informed that this project will not be expensive and is quite feasible. As t<3 this I venture no opinion at all, this is simply the information given to me, and I give it for what it is worth, I do not cite it as accurate or definite. But let us take the worst view of the case and let us suppose that it is not possible in the meantime to have a connection between the two sides of the river at Quebec. Then we are faced with the question: What are we going to do in the meantime? I am not prepared to say at this moment what we should do and what action might be taken, if indeed any action can be taken. But I take issue with the hon. the leader of the oppositon (Mr. R. L. BoTden) on his statement that this was an opportunity to exact from the Grand Trunk Pacific some modification of the contract that we have

with them. I take issue also upon his statement repeated during this debate that this transaction as to which we are asking the assent of parliament is a modification of or departure from the terms of the contract. I say on the contrary that the present loan which we make to the Grand Trunk Pacific is no departure whatever from the terms of the contract. The contract is not changed, it remains just as it was, there is no modification, this is simply an advance which we make to the company and which is to be recouped within a certain time. It is on all fours with the similar transaction of 1884 between the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was not suggested at that time or since that the loan of $30,000,000 made by the government to the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1884 implied any modification of the contract made in 1881. If it wms any modification, the changes were not material and the essence of the contract was certainly not modified. In this matter, so far as we are concerned, we intend to have no modification of the contract. It may be that in order to provide for the traffic which will originate in the west we may have seriously to consider how it is to be taken to the sea, but what I have to propose to niy hon. friend is that this was not the occasion or the opportunity to do so. The one thing in which we are concerned at this moment is to have the prairie section constructed with all speed so that the grain of the western country can be taken to the lakes this fall if possible My hon. friend rather suggested to us that we should take advantage of the dire necessity of the company to impose conditions upon it which it might or might not be prepared to accept. I must say that we did not think that this was an occasion to put such a condition upon the company. We felt on the contrary that the only thing we had to do at the present time was to see that the prairie section was completed in the shortest possible time._ At a later time we will have to discuss with the company and make some arrangement with them in reference to the matter which my hon. friend has brought up, but we. have simply to submit that this was not the occasion nor the opportunity to do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I very greatly regret that the importance of the difficulty,
I might say of the misfortune which seems imminent, so far as the Canadian ports are concerned, has not impressed itself more strongly upon the mind of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. He seems to have a very tender regard indeed for the Grand Trunk Railway Company, but he does not seem to have an equally tender nund for the interest of Canadian ports for whose benefit ostensibly this contract was made and these statutes passed. The Grand Trunk Railway Company undertook the financing of this road to a certain ex-Sir WILFRID LA DRIER.
tent. The government has performed its part of the contract, the government, the country, has not asked any modification of the contract so far as I am aware. There has been a modification, not a formal modification of the contract but a practical modification-I repeat it notwithstanding the disclaimer of the right hon. gentleman. According to his view if this country made a contract with the Grand Trunk Railway by a separate agreement to provide every single dollar of the money for the completion of that road there would be no modification of the contract. Would any man in his senses say that such is a practical view of the situation? Of course there is a modification of the contract from a practical standpoint. I think that this contract has beeen drafted and this Bill prepared in order that my hon. friends on the treasury benches may be enabled to-say : ' There is no modification in the contract/ We are providing for $10,000,000 more to be raised on the credit of this country and yet there is no modification of the contract! How is it there is nomodification of the contract when this country, by the passing of this statute, will be obliged to raise $10,000,000 more than it would otherwise have been obliged to raise for the construction of this railway? How is it possible for any reasonable man to say under these circumstances that there is no practical modification of the contract? There is not a formal modification I admit, but from a practical standpoint there certainly is a modification to this extent. Canada is raising $10,000,000 more for the construction of this railway than it would have been obliged to do if this statute had not passed.
What does my hon. friend Sir Wilfrid haulier say? He says that he regrets the Quebec bridge has fallen and admits it cannot he reconstructed before 1915. But in the meantime where is the traffic to go? Well, it is to go apparently wherever the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway will take it; and that, according to admissions of the right hon. gentleman, which I have under my hand and can quote if desired, must go to Portland, and the absolute purpose and intent of this parliament will thus be defeated during those five years at least. My right hon. friend says no, we cannot move a finger, this is not a favourable opportunity. When does he expect a favourable opportunity, if this is not one? What is to be done about it? I have his own statement that if traffic goes to North Bay, that traffic will go to Portland. I have the statement made at a Grand Trunk Railway meeting in 1903 or 1904 that the object and design of the Grand Trunk Railway was to carry that freight by the lake ports. Well, if freight reaching North Bay must be carried to Portland, can any reasonable man say that freight going to Midland

will not go to Portland also? There is absolutely no answer. Yet my right hon. friend says we must not take advantage of the dire necessity of the Grand Trunk Railway, and that this is not a favourable opportunity. But what about the dire necessity of this country? What about the necessities of the Canadian seaports of St. John and Halifax? Does regard for the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway bulk so largely in the minds of my hon. friends on the treasury benches that there is absolutely no consideration for our maritime ports? I think that the answer given by the Prime Minister is a most remarkable one, if you can dignify it by that name. There is in it not one suggestion for avoiding the imminence of the danger to which I have alluded and of which there is absolute proof.
My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) said that the carriage of this freight over the Intercolonial Railway at a small loss would not be in the interests of the people. Perhaps I do him an injustice, but at all events he said it would not be in the interests of the bookkeeping of the Intercolonial Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I did not say that. What I said was this: My hon. friend said the Intercolonial Railway ought to carry it even at a loss. I replied that if the government decided to make an arrangement to carry that traffic that way, the country as a whole ought to stand the loss and not charge it directly to the Intercolonial Railway.
That is the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Pardon me, I made the further plea that something which is donei for the country as a whole ought not to be charged to the Intercolonial Railway particularly, but the Intercolonial Railway ought to be paid as any other railway would be, -for carrying goods for the country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The net result is that it would be a mere matter of bookkeeping, and I would like to point out that experiments have been made in this, connection already. Experiments were made in 1904, during the six months preceding the 1st of March, 1904, and the net result was this:	There were five
cargoes of grain carried by the Intercolonial Railway for delivery in the elevators for export. One shipment of 16,000 bushels of wheat was carried from Depot Harbour to Halifax at the rate of 5 15 cents per bushel. Another shipment of 31.836 bushels was carried at the rate of 4 -90. Another of 39,990 bushels was carried at a rate of 5-40 cents per bushel. Another of 25,718i bushels of corn was carried at 4-94 cents per bushel. And still another of 33,892) bushels of corn was carried at 5 cents per bushel. The Intercolonial received a very small proportionate part of the rate. It did not rceeive a portion of the rate commensurate with the length of its haul. The Intercolonial Railway carried that grain 828 miles, the Grand Trunk Railway 34 miles, and the Canada Atlantic Railway, 346 miles. The percentages are given of the different shipments which I need not go over, but the net result was that the Intercolonial Railway received 2-25 cents per bushel for a haul of 828 miles and the other roads received 2-75 per bushel for a haul of 380 miles. In answer to a question put by Mr. Kemp, then member for one of the Toronto divisions, the Minister of Railways said:
The estimate of the cost per bushel for the service performed by the Intercolonial Railway was 2-27 cents and the amount received was 2:25. There was thus a slight loss on the export business; but having regard to inward cargoes and passengers obtained for the Intercolonial Railway, the business was not considered unprofitable.
Well, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways will observe that if there had been a proportionate mileage division of the rate in respect of those shipments, the Intercolonial Railway would have received 3-4 cents and the other roads 1-6 per bushel. Then as the cost of hauling to the Intercolonial Railway was 2'27 per bushel, and the proportionate amount which ought to have been received, under a fair division was 3-4, there would have been a fairly reasonable profit to the Intercolonial Railway on that haul. I am not suggesting that the Intercolonial Railway ought to make any profit upon such business, but that the interests, not of the maritime provinces alone, but of the entire Dominion, would require that the Intercolonial Railway should carry that freight to the maritime ports during the winter months at a low rate in order to prevent channels of trade being created for our western traffic to Portland and the other ports in the United States. This will be a subject of such transcendent importance during the next four or five years following the completion of the Port Arthur branch and the western division of the Transcontintal, that it was the duty of the government to have faced that difficulty just as the Grand Trunk Railway and Grand Trunk Pacific are facing their difficulties by making this application to the government. I know of no more favourable opportunity in which to press for an agreement such as I suggest. Are the interests of the country not to be considered at all? Are the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway to be always paramount? The interests of these railway corporations are entitled to just treatment on all points, but when the

government, owing to conditions over which it has at present no control-and I shall say nothing as to any default of theirs in that regard-sees that traffic gathered up in the west upon a road practically built by this government is to be carried to Portland and possibly other ports in the United States instead of to our own ports, should it not follow the example of these corporations and face that difficulty in order that some reasonable, fair and just agreement might be arrived at to safeguard the interests of our Canadian seaports ? Our only answer is in the words of the Prime Minister that we must not take any advantage of the dire necessity of this company, and that this is not a favourable opportunity for introducing this subject to their attention. Again I ask, if this is not a favourable opportunity, when does the government anticipate, in the ordinary course of events, that a favourable opportunity will arise, and what do they propose to do about it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When I spoke of ' opportunity ' and ' occasion ' I did not say the occasion was favourable or unfavourable. I said this was neither the occasion nor the opportunity. I stated a moment ago that this loan which we are making involves no .modification of the contract we have with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. My hon. friend cannot dispute that, but speaks of a 'practical modification.' Even to that extent, I think, he is in the wrong; there is no practical modification of the contract. The contract is there. We ask parliament to authorize us to make a loan of $10,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I assume that the terms of the loan will be acceptable to the company. With the exception of that loan, the government and the company will remain as they are, just as when, in 1884, the parliament authorized the government of that day to make a loan of $30,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which loan was recouped before the time it was due. There is no change of relation between the government and the company; they remain the same as if the loan had not taken place. If the loan is recouped as intended in the contract, and as I assume it will be, the relations of the government and the company will remain just as if the loan had not taken place; there is no modification of the contract whatever. But, though there is no modification of the contract, my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) says: 'You should have taken advantage of the company and should have forced upon them a modification as to the routing of the traffic that is to be developed in the Northwest.' I have simply this to say: This is not the occasion. The object at the present time, the paramount thing to do, the paramount Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
duty of the government and the country, is to see that the prairie section, which is the most important part of the road, shall be completed this year, so that the settlers who are now flocking in may have the advantage afforded by the carrying capacity of the railway. But my hon. friend in his remarks pointed out that that would be an opportunity and an occasion for the discussion of these matters. He pointed out that the contract we made in 1903 provides that when the road is completed it is to be leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. But in 1904 we put in another provision, to the effect that the commissioners who are to build the eastern section may lease some portions of the road as they are completed. They can lease the section between Moncton and Quebec or the section between Quebec and Winnipeg, and, earlier than all this, they can lease to the company the section between Winnipeg and the junction with the branch of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company connecting with Lake Superior. If we are to make a lease of that kind, that will be the opportunity and the occasion to make the arrangement which we think ought to be made for the routing of the traffic. That will be the time and the opportunity. I repeat that it would have been bad policy and bad politics to endanger the possibility of building the prairie section this year in order to make the modification in the contract which may take place later on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Surely the Prime Minister remembers that the very section to which he has alluded contains these words:
Pending the completion of the eastern division by the government, the company shall he entitled to lease from the commissioners, to be appointed under the said Act, and to operate such portions of the eastern division as may from time to time be completed, but upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the company and the said commission, which terms are not to be more onerous than those of the lease of the whole division by the said contract provided for.
Then, if they are not to be more onerous, how is he to insert such a stipulation as he speaks of? What will be the nature of that stipulation? If you frame that lease according to the provision of the statute, and the agreement, you will not advance the position one iota. Because, I repeat, what some hon. gentlemen in this House have forgotten, that this government deliberately voted down our proposal to compel the Grand Trunk Railway Com-'pany to be bound by those provisions of this contract which prevent the routing of traffic to ports other than Canadian ports. What hold will the government have upon the Grand Trunk at that time? It will not

be dealing with the Grand Trunk, but with the Grand Trunk Pacific. They are in effect, but not in form dealing with the Grand Trunk at this time, because $7,000,000 of this loan, said to have been advanced by the Grand Trunk to the Grand Trunk Pacific is to be paid out of the proceeds of the loan now proposed. Make that lease in the terms provided by that statute and when the traffic gets to Port Arthur, it will go on to Midland, and at Midland the condition which the right hon. gentleman has described with regard to North Bay will prevail-that traffic must go to Portland, and it will not go to a * Canadian port during the winter months at least. If the right hon. gentleman will explain how, on the occasion to which he has referred, he can obtain any hold upon the Grand Trunk to compel them to do that which is not only just, having regard to this whole enterprise, but which is absolutely necessary in the interests of the country as a whole, I shall be, glad to hear that explanation. But, in the light of the contract and the provisions of this contract which the government mus-tj observe, I, for one, do not know in what better position the government will be at that time than at present.
Is that only an option of the Company?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) is right. I pointed that out before, and did not think it necessary to emphasize it again. It is the company that lias the option of leasing, and the govern-1! ment have no power to compel a lease.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 1 carry?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Carried.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If my right hon. friend's answer to this is simply ' carried,' I do not think the country will be satisfied with that answer.

I have great respect for the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his statement, but for the life of me I cannot see on what reasonable basis he argues that there is no modification of this contract. He says that there is no modification, because we are only lending money to the railway company. We made this bargain in 1903. The country was to carry out a certain part of the building of the Tailway and the company was to do a certain other part. They came to us in 1904 and obtained modifications. I do not think the right hon. Prime Minister will say that those were not important modifications. The result of those two contracts is that, so far as the western division is concerned, we were to guarantee three-fourths of the ex pense of building the prairie section, not exceeding $13,000 per mile; the Grand
Trunk Railway Company-because it was the Grand Trunk Railway Company that was invariably put forth as being the substantial contractor-was to do all the rest; absolutely, according to the Minister of Finance, and according to the leader of the government, the old Grand Trunk Railway Company was practically to do all the Test. We were to put our guarantee to three-fourths of the necessary money, and nominally the Grand Trunk Pacific was to finance the rest of the scheme, and to have its bonds endorsed by the Grand Trunk Company. Have they dene that? No doubt we have done our part, every iota of our bargain has been fulfilled; and if they were not now asking for a modification of the bargain, would they be coming here at all? It is because the Grand Trunk Railway Company has not endorsed the bonds that it was to guarantee, according to the bargain that they entered into with the Dominion of Canada, that they are coming here to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They will endorse those bonds.

That is not the bargain. The Minister of Finance will recognize that he cannot blow hot and cold on this matter. He says this contract is entirely separate from the old contract, and therefore they are not carrying out the old contract in endorsing these bonds, they are not guaranteeing them under that contract. The reason they are coming here is because, instead of guaranteeing those bonds, they have gone into some other scheme. In some way oi other the Grand Trunk Company has, for the time being, obtained a temporary loan, and they have put $7,000,000 into this road. They do not want to endorse those bonds because it would impair their credit. But they thought they would form some scheme by which to tide over until after the elections, and then they would come to us and ask this parliament to provide funds, and so modify the agreement entered into in 1903 and 1904, instead of endorsing those bonds according to agreement. Is it not idle to talk about modifications under such circumstances? If the Grand Trunk Railway Company were carrying out the agreement they solemnly entered into with parliament, there would be no application here at all, there could not be any application here, because the bonds would be endorsed, the money would have been obtained, and this loan would not be- required. The Minister of Finance says: 'Oh, we have nothing to do with the Grand Trunk Company; it is not the Grand Trunk Company we are dealing with at all. it is the Grand Trunk Pacific Company we are dealing with, and we do not need to pay any attention as to where this money is to go, we have only to ascertain that it has gone into the road.' But up to this time he has not found out whether it has gone into the road or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has not gone anywhere yet.

Yes it has, if the statements presented to parliament are true, because we have it in black and white that $7,000,000 has actually been put into the road, that is now required to be paid to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. You cannot conceal the fact from the members of this House nor from the people of this country, that it is the Grand Trunk Company that is coming forward to get this loan at the present time; it is not the Grand Trunk Pacific, that is only a name. It has been suggested here to me that it is one and the same red-headed boy; the Grand Trunk Company is going to be the red-headed boy, and always has been. Now not only has this contract been modified in the way I have pointed out, but the right hon. gentleman will have to admit it has been modified in a much more substantial way. Not only was the Grand Trunk Company to stand behind this scheme, and be of it, and in it, and the whole thing, but as to the $25,000,000 of stock they were to hand over was every dollar of it to go into this enterprise before we could be called upon to pay a dollar. I am talking, not upon what anybody on the back benches has said, I am talking of the language of the Prime Minister himself. . When the hon. member for Hamilton complained of the fact that we were making no provision to prevent the Grand Trunk Railway Company getting this stock for nothing, the Prime Minister pointed out, after being not too complimentary in his allusions about quibbling and petty-fogging on this side of the House-he pointed out that every dollar of that $25,000,000 of stock had to go into the building of this road if it were required. Has that $25,000,000 gone into the building of this road? If it has not, I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman if he does not think that is a modification of the contract. Will he say he did not give this House explicitly to understand in 1903 and 1904 that every dollar of that $25,000,000 of stock was to go into the building of the road, if it was necessary for the building of the road? The right hon. gentle man does not claim the right to reply. I will therefore take the liberty of giving the language he used on that occasion. He says, on page 11222 of the ' Hansard ':
My hon. friend from Hamilton says that the two companies are one, and that the stock is to be taken by the Grand Trunk Railway; and he asked, How is the value to be determined between them? Well, the value is to be determined by the means of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will require money to carry on its enterprise.
It requires it now, according to the proposition before the House.

If it needs the whole $25,000,060, the amount of this capital stock at par, it will have to get it, and it can only get it from the Grand Trunk Railway. In such a case, the value of that stock will be its par value, because that will the amount which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway requires in return for its stock and which the Grand Trunk Railway will have to pay. The value of the stock will 'be fixed by the needs of the company, and cannot be fixed in any other way.
Any modification of the contract? Today we are told, if I understand the answers that are brought down, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company got that stock for a matter of $205,200, or got upwards of $24,000,000 of it. They have not put that $24,000,000 odd into this enterprise; the Prime Minister promised us that they would, if required, put it into this enterprise. Does he want to tell this committee and this country that there is no modification of the contract, when we are asked to-day to put this $10,000,000 more into this enterprise, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company has not guaranteed those bonds and has not accounted for that $24,000,000 of stock?
Yet holds it all.

Yet holds it all. It is not modification, but repudiation. It is an absolute denial of the contract. It is treating the members of this House as if they were a lot of children rather than treating them as if they were independent, reasonable men desirous of doing their duty to the people. I am amazed at the failure of the leading members of the government to appreciate the gravity of the situation we are confronted with at the present time. I need not read-my honoured leader read them this afternoon-the forty-second and forty-third sections of the contract by which it was expressly stipulated that, as a paramount consideration that we would obtain the development of Canadian ports and receive an absolute guarantee that the great products of the west would be shipped outwards by Canadian ports. I am amazed at the fact that in face of that condition of things the government have to come down and acknowledge that they have not taken the first step, that they have not uttered the first syllable in order to try and implement the promise made to the people by that agreement, the main plank in the proposition that the right hon. gentleman launched in this House in the summer of 1903. It was for the purpose of developing Canadian ports and seeing to it that Canadian products were carried entirely on Canadian soil and upon an all-Canadian line that we were asked to pledge our credit and enter into what was said to be, great enterprise. In face of the fact that it has become absolutely impossible that we can hold the

Grand Trunk Pacific to their contract, as contained in section 20, -which provided that they should take a lease of this line when it was entirely completed, and in face of the fact that it is manifest that until 1915 we cannot make the connection necessary to complete the line, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Finance Minister have not risen to the opportunity which they have now, and which they lost before. Having another opportunity presented to them, they have been recreant to their duty to the people. They have not seized the occasion to obtain a inodification of the agreement. It is not for the Prime Minister to boast that there is no modification of the agreement, but he should have been proud to say:	'We have obtained a modification by which we secured the traffic down to Canadian ports, which otherwise, by reason of the disaster of the Quebec bridge, would necessarily have been diverted to Portland.' It was not only the duty of the government upon this occasion to have made it absolutely clear before we undertook to give this money that some arrangement would be made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company by which substantially the original contract would be carried out; but it was the duty of the government to have done more than that. It was the duty of the government, when that bridge fell and when they realized that it would he years and years before it could be restored, to have taken steps to see that we would not have millions of money lying idle in that road for yeaTS to come, the road depreciating from year to year and the government and the people absolutely helpless to compel the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific to take over any portion of the line. As has been pointed out, it is manifest that subsection 3 of the new contract of 1904 is a fug-handled arrangement, just like the British preference. It is ail on one side-option to the company, an option which gives the government no power to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to take over any portion of this line, unless they will it, until every part of the line is absolutely completed. I have no hesitation of charging the government in the most explicit and definite way with a neglect of duty not only on the present occasion, but 'neglect of duty' dating farther back than that, namely, to the time when they had the right to foresee that by reason of the fall of the Quebec bridge some new terms ought to be sought, and in the absence of the making of a satisfactory arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific the building of a portion of the line should have been suspended for such a time that its completion would be about coincident of the completion of the new bridge. To what purpose 168
are we spending our millions on the extreme eastern portion of the line if until 1915 we cannot possible use it? Is it to the benefit of the country; is it to the benefit of the people of the maritime provinces, because if it were I would not complain? Is it to the benefit of any one that the line should, as the government practically propose now, absolutely remain idle for five years, paying large amounts of interest, not less than $10,000,000, during the time it is idle, or would it have been common sense, common prudence, for the government first to have seen what arrangement they could make with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and, failing this arrangement, to have said:	'It is idle for us to invest our
money; we will not break faith with the maritime provinces, but we will suspend operations and so arrange the work that the completion of the bridge and the completion of the eastern end of the Transcontinental Railway shall be, as nearly as possible, coincident?' But for the fact that I want to emphasize that we should not be called upon to advance this money at this time, I do not like to quote what has been so often quoted in this House-the language of the Prime Minister and the.Finance Minister in particular as to the position of the Grand Trunk in this matter. * On second thought, and I think it is the best thought, I will not do it now. If I hear much more of this repudiation I will be compelled, in justice, to do so. Let me just say at this .moment that I will only refer to the expression used a few moments ago by the Prime Minister when he said: 'What was the paramount duty of the government?' The paramount duty of the government was to see to the early completion of this line and of the prairie section so as to bring the grain from the west to enable it to be transported to the sea and then to the markets of the world. Yes, that is a duty, but the paramount duty in this case was to impress upon the Grand Trunk Company that they should keep their contract with parliament. By reason of the laxity of the government in not securing tht transportation of this freight over the Intercolonial Railway, instead of having more western freight brought over an all-Caradian line to Canadian ports, moTe of it than ever will go through American channels, and the declaration which the Prime Minister made with such gusto in 1903 in that respect will be altogether falsified.

How does the Minister of Finance reconcile the statement that the Grand Trunk are applying for this loan because they do not desire to place their bonds on the market, with the fact that $7,000,000 has already been raised and is owing bv the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Grand Trunk Railway? I would further



ask, if the Grand Trunk do not desire to place their bonds in the market at the present time, why is it that between the date of the letter written by Mr. Hays and the present time they have applied for power to borrow $12,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no doubt that
the loan which they have obtained power to raise will not be placed on the market until a later date when the conditions will be deemed favourable. I do not know how the Grand Trunk Railway obtained the $7,000,000, but I would suppose it was either from the ordinary revenue of the Grand Trunk or through their bankers in the ordinary process. If that be the case, they would have to recoup the bankers by selling the bonds; and tojdo that they will have to place them on the market at a sacrifice. I do not see any difficulty in reconciling the two things.
I assume the company would not ask for power to- borrow $12,000,000 more unless they were going to place that loan on the market in the near future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The correspondence speaks for itself.
That is a reply which is open to the right hon. gentleman; and it is open to the House and to the country to interpret it and to draw their own inference.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is a free country.

The right hon. gentleman prides himself on his frankness, and the very fact that he is unable to say that the first intimation came on the 16th of November, tells its own tale. Will the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister be frank enough to answer this question-when the $10,000,000 loan was mooted between the parties, did the government know or did they try to find out how the money put Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
into the construction before the 16th of November was raised by the Grand Trunk Company?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Minister of Railways might be able to inform my hon. friend, but I certainly cannot.

It is a great pity the Minister of Railways is not here when we are discussing this very important question. VVill the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance answer another question- did any member of the government or the government as a whole assist the Grand Trunk Railway Company in getting, as accommodation or as an advance, that large amoun of money from the bank to tide them over until this legislation could be put through?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there was any such understanding. We were aware that the Grand Trunk Company, no being ready to issue the bonds, was advancing money to assist this enterprise. As to the particular method they took to raise the money I never had any information, nor did I think it necessary to inquire. I cannot answer in any other terms.
You cannot answer more explicitly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. If I could have done anything to help them I would have been very glad to do so, but there was no need. The Grand Trunk raised the money, but as to the particular manner in which they raised it I have no information. I would gladly assist the Grand Trunk if it were necessary, but so far as I know they got it on their own credit entirely.

Are we to understand then that the government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, knew nothing about this, had entered into no arrangement and no agreement at an earlier date than is shown by this correspondence? The government know whether they did or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was no obligation to raise this money and there is not yet; it is an absolutely onen matter for parliament to determine whether we shall raise this money now or not. It was a subject of conversation between representatives of the Grand Trunk and ourselves, and we were aware that they were temporarily raising money and assisting in the prosecution of the work, and we understood they would have to issue bonds to raise the money. The question whether they should issue the bonds, going on the market themselves, or we should do it was discussed and it was decided to bring down this resolution.
How long before the 16th of November was that quasi-arrangement with the company made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not consider it a quasi-arrangement. There is no obligation yet which is binding on any one. It this is not a good transaction we are free not to complete it.
Could the minister tell about what time the negotiations commenced which ended in this arrangement and the bringing before parliament of this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not tell.
The minister could not tell?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Is money so small a thing, does the minister take so little stock *of it and of the obligations which he is placing on the country that a $10,000,000 transaction slips out of his mind and that he does not remember when it was broached?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been no $10,000,000 transaction. Had we assumed an obligation for $10,000,000, there would certainly be some record of it, but that obligation does not yet exist.

If a neighbour came to my hon. friend and asked him for a loan of $1,000 or $10,000 it would have impressed itself on his memory sufficiently to make a mark and he would be able to tell a month afterwards about what time the friend asked him for the loan. Here comes another friend, a pampered friend, and asks for a $10,000,000 loan. Is he so accustomed to dealing with the country's millions that this made no impression on .his great mind and that to-day he cannot tell when it occurred?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have told my hon. friend all about it.
Of course if the Prime Minister had forgotten it is his duty to forget, but it is the duty of the man who has the finances of the country in his charge to remember.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We still have the money, so there is no barm done.
I would not say that that is quibbling, because the chairman might object, hut it is mightly close to quibbling.

I notice in a letter of the manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific that he says the Grand Trunk has already guaranteed bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the extent of $30,000,000. Will the minister say whether or not the guaranty of the present loan will stand on the same footing as the guaranty by the Grand Trunk of the Grand Trunk Pacific bonds as against the Grand Trunk Pacific? Will we have a greater right to payment from the 1681
Grand Trunk Pacific than the Grand Trunk will have against the Grand Trunk Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not like to answer these questions off-hand, but my ipipression is it will stand in the same position as other guarantees by the Grand Trunk Pacific.

So the position we are in so far as the Grand Trunk is concerned is that we have $121,000,000 of guaranteed bonds ahead of us, $19,000,000 of rentals capitalized at 4 per cent and $12,000,000, which we granted them power to issue this year, all of which will be prior to our guaranty, and after that we only stand in the same position as the Grand Trunk Pacific do in respect of their $30,000,000 which the Grand Trunk has guaranteed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: T presume my hon. friend's figures are correct. I have not made the additions.
I understand there-are also some $6,000,000 equipment morh, gage bonds outstanding against the Grand Trunk which are also a prior lien to the-present loan or guaranty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think all these securities are included in the sum which I mentioned at a previous stage of the debate, as the amount which would come ahead of our guaranty and which will leave, as we claim, a surplus which will be ample to protect our guaranty.

I do not know whether the $121,000,000 will be sufficient to cover the bonds of the Grand Trunk or not but that certainly does not include the) $19,000,000 of rentals capitalized nor the $12,000,000 we have allowed them to borrow this year. That makes $152,000,000 ahead of this guaranty and then we only stand to take our share of anything that re mains with the other 30 million bonds that are guaranteed by the Grand Trunk.

I do not see why five years should be consumed in building even the great bridge at Quebec. I believe that bridge can be built in two yeajs or perhaps less. Then other means can be adopted, a ferry can be built and it must be remembered that the Intercolonial is an important factor in the situation and that nothing must be done with the Intercolonial that will prevent it from being utilized. Then it may be possible to cross the river further to the west and so keep the traffic in this country. I would emphasize that we can never depend on private enterprise for the realizing of a great national policy. We have put ourselves, as I have said this afternoon, in the hands of a private corporation to realize a great national policy, a policy that is to build up our own ports and our own country, and to

keep our own traffic in Canada. I repeat that this is bad policy, it is not a true national policy and yet this road was supposed to be built on national lines. The government must find a way to build this bridge in less than five years. Of course if you give it to a commission, and the commission wish to prolong their tenure of office they can extend it over for quite a while. But great bridges now are being built in a year and two years. The river at New York has been spanned twice now by enormous bridges costing $20,000,000 in a great deal less than two years and the same thing can be done in this case. It is imcumbent upon the government to find a way to overcome the situation in the shortest possible time.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I fully agree with my hon. friend. In reference to the New York bridges I might suggest that one of them was built but has not yet been used, unless it was within the last week or two, as itl was found to be defective.
It was opened the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The investigation into the fall of the Quebec bridge led to investigations into that bridge, and it was not accepted, unless very recently. I may say that while I have not taken exception to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition as to the time for the building of the Quebec bridge, the building of the Quebec bridge is under the Railway Department and will be pushed with all possible speed, commensurate with getting a safe substantial bridge. We want a bridge that will stay there when constructed. If it can be completed in two years it will be.

Is the government aware of the currency of a story that a considerable proportion of the indebtedness of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the Grand Trunk Railway arises out of the fact that material is supplied by the latter to the former? I ask that because it has a bearing on the representations that we are to get a road of exceptionally high standard. But if 80 lb. rails have been taken off the line of the Grand Trunk Railway, to be replaced by 100 lb. rails, and if these old rails are placed on the Grand Trunk Pacific, of course we are being deceived as to the character of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned that. The only transaction that could give rise to that story is this: I believe that the Grand Trunk Pacific has taken for its sidings some 80 lb. rails, which are in good condition, from the Grand Trunk Railway. The 80 lb. rails are practically just as good Mr. W. P. MACLEAN.
as the others for the purposes of sidings. The Grand Trunk Railway is replacing its 80 lb. rails on its main line by 100 lb. rails, and is furnishing the Grand Trunk Pacific with these 80 lb. rails for the purposes of sidings only in a limited quantity.
Is any part of the purchase price a part of that $7,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say that.

Has this reason been advanced to the government as a reason for making this loan, that the Grand Trunk Railway were embarrassed by the fact that they have undertaken to pay the government upon the cost of the Winnipeg and Moncton division 3 per cent per year, and that since this division is to cost a great deal more than twice the sum they were led to believe it would, their liability is now 6 per cent instead of three per cent on the sum originally estimated, and on which they depended owing to the confidence with which the government made that estimate. It would be impossible for any railway company to pay a rental of 6 per cent on a road when their expectation was that they would only have to pay 3 per cent, when there is no expectation that the traffic will be increased by one ton by this additional cost.
