Have they come to the government representing that that they are burdened by a liability which they foolishly assumed without knowing the actual cost, and so consequently do not wish to issue bonds upon their own responsibility, but want the government to issue bonds for them. This leads to the further supposition that it must be clear to the government that never will the Grand Trunk Pacific pay the 3 per cent that now stands as part of the contract. We ought to know definitely whether it is contemplated that at a future day we shall be asked to relieve the company of that three per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No member of the government has ever heard any suggestion or proposal such as my hon. friend has indicated.
Is it the expectation of the government that the Grand Trunk Pacific will, at the proper time, commence the payment of the three per cent?

That is what the contract calls for, and I have never heard them question their obligation. They entered into the contract; it was a pretty hard one. Hon. gentlemen opposite pretended that it was a most favourable contract for the Grand Trunk Railway, and I have never heard that company make any suggestion regarding shirking any obligation under it.

My hon. friend the Finance Minister says that not a dollar will

be paid for any work done until he has the certificate of his chief engineer. But how far back will the engineer go? Suppose a claim be made for $7,000,000, what kind of a certificate is the engineer going to give? Take the ties, for instance, that go into the road. The engineer is told that so many ties have gone into it and he satisfies himself that that number of ties has really gone into the road. The company say that these ties have cost, let us say 60 cents, and lay the vouchers before the engineer. Does the engineer go any further back or does he simply take these vouchers and base his certificate on them as regards the cost? It might happen that these ties went through three or four hands before being placed on the road. The first contractor might have got the contract at 60 cents. Then he sublets that contract say at 50 cents. The sub-contractor goes a little further down and gets them supplied at 40 cents. Then away down at the bottom, the man who takes them off the stump is paid, say 30 cents. Has the engineer the right to go back and find out what the ties cost from the stump?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that the ties are obtained by public tender and contract. If tenders were advertised for and contracts awarded after public competition, it would not be the business of the engineer to follow the ties back to the woods. That which is obtained in open competition may fairly be taken as a standard price. Besides, the chief engineer has several assistants who live along the line of the railway and who watch its whole construction and report as often as is necessary. These would know and the chief engineer, even at this distance would, from his long experience, know the value of the ties. In the first place the company present their statement. Then there is an audit made of the vouchers and the books, and the auditor must be satisfied that these amounts are correct, as a mere matter of accounting. If there be an item which should not properly be charged to that service, the auditor from his experience and knowledge criticises that item, and certifies to what is correct. Then comes the question whether the charges are fair and reasonable. The chief engineer, through his general knowledge of railway construction and the information he is continually receiving from his assistant engineers, has to decide that point. He has to decide on the value of the ties, the cost of the rails, the cost of labour, the cost of moving so many yards of earth, and he certifies whether these charges are fair and reasonable. That is the method of auditing and certifying.
Did the hon. minister say that the sidings were being laid with old rails taken from the Grand Trunk Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The statement made was, as I understood, that a certain quantity had to be used in that way.
Second-hand rails?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They might be secondhand rails, strictly speaking, and be absolutely as good for the sidings as new rails. They would have been used for many years if the Grand Trunk had not taken them up to make way for 100-pound rails. For all purposes, they will last longer on the sidings than new rails on the main line.
But are they secondhand rails? And are they first-class secondhand rails, or wha.t quality are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I understand that they are rails in first-class condition.

In connection with the statement made by the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) just now when questioned as to whether the prices were fair and reasonable, I would remind the committee of a little matter that came before this House a couple of years ago in regard to one of the contracts made by one of the contractors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. During the discussion of the Robbins irrigation case, it was shown that an English company had taken over the assets of the company and also the assets of the Grand Forks Cattle Company. Amongst these assets appeared a contract for the supplying of meat to the contractors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. When the assets were valued, the valuator spoke of this contract in the following terms:
I am prepared to say that a very moderate estimate of the value of this contract would be from $50,000 to $75,000.
And the Southern Alberta Land Company actually paid to the Grand Forks Cattle Company $50,000 for the benefit of this contract which they took over, and, I suppose, carried out. It seems to me that that shows that very extravagant prices were being paid at that time. The gentlemen who composed the Grand Forks Cattle Company were Messrs. J. D. McGregor, Brandon; D. A. Ross, Vancouver; A. E. Hitchcock, Moosejaw, and others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was this contract for the construction of a section of the road?
It was for supplying meat to the contractors of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not, then, touch the company itself. Assuming that the contract is let by tender, whether the contractor pays a high price or a low price for his supplies cannot affect the railway company. We are not concerned in following the case back to find out what the

contractor paid for his supplies. The sum of $50,000 would not necessarily be a large amount of money to make out of a contract in connection with the construction of a railway. Everything would turn on the volume of the business done.

Have the government discussed with the Grand Trunk Pacific in any way the idea of transferring to the government the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific to be held by the government until the loan is paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In my judgment, the taking of the stock as additional security would be of no value, as at present the stock has little or no' commercial value itself. The common stock 'of a company building a railway that is only one-half, or less, completed can hardly be regarded as, at the moment, a very valuable security. It may become valuable in time. But should it .become valuable, it can only be when the company's obligations have been met, and the meeting of the company's obligations would make our holding of the stock unnecessary. The fact that this stock has become valuable would be the best evidence that the obligations which the company have incurred were paid and the whole concern in a flourishing condition. Therefore, we should not get anything of value to us by taking the common stock.

I would not suggest that the common stock would now be any security to the government in connection with the loan. At the same time, I do not agree with the Minister of Finance in what he has said. This stock at present has no market value to the government in case these bonds are not paid, hut we all know the difficulty there is when there is a default on the bonds of a railway. Proceedings would have to be gone through in order to get possession of the road. That case has arisen many times. The agreements made by parliament, especially in 1904, are very bad in that respect. That agreement provides that if the bonds guaranteed by the government are not paid, a receiver is to be appointed, and the receiver, if he has any money left after he pays the working expenses of the railway, simply has to divide that money pro rata between the holders of the first mortgage bonds and the holders of the second mortgage bonds so-called. In this case, the government is providing further money for this railway, and I do not suggest their taking this stock as security, but as a mere matter of proper care on the part of the government. The fact that, as the Minister of Finance said, the stock is of no present value is no reason, it seems to me, why it should not be transferred to the government to be held until the bonds are paid. Many not only in this House but in the country think that, as the people of Mr. FIEBDING.
Canada have to pay so much, they should have some of the stock of this company, to own it in perpetuity for themselves. That is one question that has been raised. But the question I raise is simply that of taking this stock and holding it until the debt is paid, so that, if there is a default the government may own the stock of the railway subject, of course, to the other liabilities, and may be able to administer it without going through the long course of litigation and trouble in case of default.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are of opinion tha^ the machinery to protect the government is all that is necessary, and that the proposition to take over the common stock is of no value to us.

Would the hon. ministei argue that, in case there is default in thf payment of these bonds, this $10,000,000 which the government is advancing, the government would not be in a better position to deal with the difficulties and to handle the road if it had this stock in its own name, rather than go through the process of law necessary to have the road foreclosed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are many interests involved in the road, and I think that if we take the usual method of protecting these respective classes of investors, we shall not go wrong. I think the hon. member magnifies the difficulties of enforcing the lien. I have no doubt that under the machinery provided, we can exercise as effective control as we could by the possession of the common stock. Anyhow, the Grand Trunk Company, by statute, is the owner of that stock. I do not think any advantage could come to us by asking the common stock to be put up as an additional security.
Is the minister right in saying that the Grand Trunk is by statute the owner of that stock ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. Originally we required the Grand Trunk to acquire and hold that stock, we stipulated that they should hold it. One criticism that was offered was that it was a scheme by which individuals could get possession of this common stock, and put it on the stock market and speculate in it to their own personal gain, and we stipulated that the Grand Trunk should acquire and hold that stock.
In 1904 we stipulated something else. The statute of 1904 pro vided that the Grand Trunk Railway Company could dispose, I think, of more than half of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had forgotten that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The agreement of 1904 modified that of 1903. That of 1904

merely required that they should hold a majority of the stock; therefore they could dispose of more than $12,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
quote the section?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Section 9 of the agreement of 1904.

The intention at that time was that the Grand Trunk should pay for this stock. The Grand Trunk paid almost nothing for the stock. I submit that the minister should not endeavour to make the distinction between the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific in this matter. There is no difference, so far as we are concerned. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway undertakes to build this road, and the Grand Trunk undertakes to guarantee it and see it through. Whether this stock is in the hands of the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific, matters not, as we are doing a favour to both of these corporations. I may say that the taking of this stock in the name of the government, in the meantime, does no harm whatever to either the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific. It hurts nobody, because it could be transferred to the government, and at the same time the rights of the Grand Trunk Railway to vote on this stock would be protected, so they would have full control of the enterprise in the meantime. It seems to me therefore that if that stock were transferred to the government it would be a good thing for the government and do nobody any harm. If the government are not prepared to make some such arrangement, I give notice now that I propose to move an amendment on the third reading.

I would like to ask the Minister of Finance with reference to that stock that the Grand Trunk was to pay for. A small portion of that has gone to the directors, and they have paid a percentage upon it, some $200 or $400 each' on the shares they hold. The rest is held by three gentlemen in trust, I suppose, for the Grand Trunk Company. Now it has been stated that $205,000 has been paid. I see that $5,000 was paid by the directors in percentages on their total stock. But I see it stated in certain places that $205,000 has been paid on the bulk of the stock, the 249,000 shares. Does the Finance Minister know how that was paid, on what basis? Is it a percentage on the whole stock, and did that go into the road or into the treasury of the Grand Trunk Company? That is an important thing. The stock was not to go into the pockets of the Grand Trunk for nothing, its proceeds were to go into the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If any money was paid it would go into the treasury of the Grand
Trunk Pacific for that purpose. We gave the House the information furnished us by the company, and I presume it is on1 that my hon. friend is speaking. But I' could not tell by what process he reached; that basis. It was not covered by the, question, and I did not inquire closely into it.
Then will the Finance Minister, in the audit of what has gone into the road, include that sum?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Unless there was_ work to represent it we could not include it.
Then the minister does not know whether that $205,000 said to have been paid by the Grand Trunk for its stock, went into the construction of the road or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say.
Should we not have that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may have a bearing on the question; I have not thought of that.

I would like the Finance Minister to take that idea up, and have the certificate of the engineer if that $205,000 went into the actual construction of the road. For all we know, it may have gone into the coffers of the Grand Trunk, and we never made them take $25,000,000 of common stock to put into their own treasury, we gave them that stock to be used for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Then I think we have a perfect right to know whether that $205,000 represented so much cash, or so much material which absolutely went into the construe tion of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I think we should have that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the information is accessible. I did give all the information that seemed called for. If the information can be obtained I will be happy to get it.

The Finance Minister has laid down the principle that none of the money which is provided in the contract, from whatever source it came, was to be idly spent, it was all to go into the construction of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And for other purposes in connection with it, whatever might be the general expenses of management.

They have not been managing the operation of the road, they have been constructing it. It is in accord with the legislation that whatever money was paid on that stock, realized from any portion of that stock, should go into the construction of the road. Now, does the government know that it did, or has it taken any means of finding out whether it did or not? Would the minister give instructions

to the chief engineer to see whether that $205,000 went into the construction of the road or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The information I received I gave to the House. I will consider the matter.

With respect to this common stock, what liability attaches to that stock in the possession of the Grand Trunk Railway Company? We are familiar with the ordinary conditions under which a joint stock company may hold its stock on which all the calls have not been paid. If the company get into financial difficulty their creditors can come back on them for the difference between what they paid and the face value. Now, parliament made this arrangement about the common stock on the solemn assurance of the Minister of Justice, as quoted by my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo yesterday, that this common stock should not be parted with except for value. We find it has passed from the Grand Trunk Pacific for no value. The question occurs to me: What would hannen in future if the government or any other creditors wished to realize on their claims against the company, whether they could go back to the Grand Trunk as the owners of this stock and ask them to contribute the difference between what they have paid and the face value or whether they are exempt from that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I think that if my hon. friend will turn to the Act of 1904, chap. 80, he will find that it is provided that the Grand Trunk shall receive that stock in return for certain services rendered and particularly for their guarantee. I have always thought that the guarantee which the Grand Trunk has given to the Grand Trunk Pacific is the chief service that it renders. The question which my hon. friend puts to me may be a legal one that I am not competent to answer, but my impression is that the stock would be held to be non-assessable and paid up and the chief consideration that the Grand Trunk gave for it was that they guaranteed the bonds of this subsidiary company. A man who undertakes to endorse his neighbour's notes for many millions of dollars, such as are involved in this transaction, renders a very valuable service. The Grand Trunk for the moment gets no advantage from that, because, as the hon. gentleman admits, there is no immediate value in the stock, but if in the process of time the stock should become valuable that is the compensation which the Grand Trunk will receive for the tremendous aid it is granting to the younger enterprise.
Mr, BURRELL. Surely the Finance Minister would regard it as singular that we, who have guaranteed three times the amount, cannot hold that stock as collateral.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Grand Trunk like every other railway company is a soulless corporation and is looking not for glory but for dollars and cents like every other business man.
And they are getting them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In reference to that criticism I would just say that no contract that was ever made for a great enterprise in the Dominion of Canada contains so many severe restrictions upon the contracting company as will be found in this contract. Instead of being of great profit to the company I do not hesitate to say that this is a contract which imposes a great burden upon them, and they will have to wait for the progress of years and the growth and prosperity of the country before they will find their reward. But, they are looking for their reward, as all corporations and financial men are looking for it, in the tangible form of profits, if not to-day, to-morrow or a future day. But, the government is not in this enterprise for the purpose of obtaining dividends. The government is in this enterprise for the purpose of aiding in the development of the country and the gain to the government representing the country is not to come in the form of a small percentage upon some common stock, but it is to come from the development and progress of the country.
That is all very eloquent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not think it was; I thought it was very sensible.

I must pay my hon. friend the compliment of saying that it was very eloquent and, as it was intended, it brought a cheer from his followers and turned them away from the very pertinent question that my hon. friend asked. I want to ask the Prime Minister what he thinks of the statement made by the Finance Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought it was very eloquent and very true.

I agree with my right hon. friend in saying that it was veTy eloquent but what did he think of it before the Finance Minister went on with his eloquent periods? What the Finance Minister seemed to say was that this stock belonged to the Grand Trunk and that they could do what they liked with it. They were given that stock because they guaranteed or promised to guarantee certain bonds. Having promised to guarantee certain bonds and having guaranteed certain bonds this was the reward, not now realizable, but at some time in the future. How does the Prime Minister reconcile that view of the case with his own solemn statement made to this House and reiterated everywhere,

that every dollar of the stock was, if it were required, to go into the road for the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific ? Is there anything like consistency and business integrity and straightforwardness in making the investment of $180,000,000 to $200,000,000 in this property as to the basis upon which you induced the country to go into it? Was not that the very prime part of it? The Prime Minister himself, who is supposed to keep his word, who is supposed to have his government in control, who is supposed to be superior even to a corporation, pledges his word as the Prime Minister that every dollar of the stock would go into the building of the road if required, and then, a year, or two, or three years afterwards, we have the statement of the Finance Minister that the stock is not to go into the road but that it is simply the possession of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and that it was given to them in payment for their guarantees in certain directions. The Prime Minister must see that these two positions are diametrically opposed. What does he think about it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think they are at all.
I had supposed that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, my hon. friend will agree with me. I stated in 1903 that this stock would go to the building of the road. The Grand Trunk would put it to the payment of the road. The Grand Trunk have been advancing money for the carrying on of the enterprise. My hon. friend knows that we are in stringent times financially and that it is difficult to finance the bonds. The company therefore have had to come here in order to do their financing. What took place in 1884? I remember the speech which was made a few days ago by my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro). He presented a very eloquent statement and he made a comparison of the securities of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in 1884 when they came here for a loan of $30,000,000 and the securities which are offered to-day by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. He stated that on that occasion the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had offered securities which he valued at $200,000,000, consisting of the land grant, 3,000 miles of railway completed, ships and subsidies. I do not think ;that my hon. friend exaggerated when be stated that in 1884 the Canadian Pacific Railway had securities to the value of $200,000,000 to offer to bankers and financial institutions in order to get the money necessary to complete that enterprise. Yet they could not get a dollar upon those securities. It is a matter of history that the Canadian Pacific Railway at that time went to the banks and financial institutions in Canada, to the banks
and financial institutions in New York, London and Amsterdam, offered $200,000000 of securities to get $30,000,000 and they could not get one dollar. It is a matter of history also that the men who were at the head of the enterprise, George Stephen and Donald Smith, offered their own personal notes to the banks and that they got money upon their own personal notes while the banks would not take the $200,000,000 of securities. Why was that?-because it is well known that the public will not invest in such big enterprises until they have reached a certain stage when they can command confidence. That is the position in whidh we are today. The' Grand Trunk Pacific cannot without loss realize upon their bonds at present and that is why the government had to come to the aid of the company, exactly as the government came to the aid of another company in 1884. The Grand Trunk has that stock; it will become valuable, it will be worth more than par and then they will get their profit out of it, and it is only fair and reasonable they should have whatever profit may attach to the enterprise. Is it for profit or glory that men go mto an enterprise of that kind? It is for profit, and therefore I see no contradiction between my statement and the statement of the Minister of Finance.

I thank the Prime Minister for his eloquent period, but what I wanted him to do was to reconcile his position with the position of the Minister of Finance. Now let him pay attention to the plain English of what he did say, and then let him ask himself whether he meant anything or whether he was simply getting oil an eloquent period then as he has done to-night. It was at a time when he should have meant something and when he should not have let one word escape him which did not have its definite meaning and its pledge of the honour of the leader of the government behind it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let me have your reading of it now.

Yes; this is what the right hon. gentleman said:
My hon. friend from Hamilton says that the two companies are one and that the stock is to be taken by the Grand Trunk Company, and he asked how is the value bo be determined between the two companies. Well, the value is to be determined by the needs of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will require money to carry' on its enterprise. If it needs the whole $25,000,000 the amount of the capital stock at par, it will have to get it and can only get it from the Grand Trunk Railway. In such a case the value of the stock will be the par value because that will be the amount which the Grand Trunk Pa-

cific requires in return for its stock, or which the Grand Trunk Railway would have to pay. The value of the stock will be fixed by the needs of the company and cannot be fixed in any other way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think that was badly put at all.
I think it was very straightly put.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, Hear.

It is not that I quarrel with the right hon. gentleman that he has not put things straight; I quarrel with him because he does not keep straight to the straight way in which he puts things. That is what I have been trying to impress upon him for a great many, years, but I have absolutely failed. The *debt hon. gentleman will get up to-day and he will put a thing as straight as the English language ean put it, so that you can take but one meaning out of it, but he does not keep to that. There is no other meaning to be taken from this language than that this stock being in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway its value was to be determined bv the needs of the Grand Trunk Pacific; if the Grand Trunk Pacific needed $25,000,000, par was to be the rate, and it was to be given by the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific needed $9,000,000 of that now. According to the statement of the right hon. gentleman who is the father of the scheme, when the Grand Trunk Pacific needed that money it was to go to the Grand Trunk Railway who had that stock, and on the basis of par it was to demand it. It got its $10,000,000, or nearly so, from the Grand Trunk Railway, but the Grand Trunk Railway has a halter round the neck of my right hon. friend, metaphorically speaking, and the Grand Trunk Railway proposes to keep this stock and to make the government do its financing, and so it pulled the string a little tight at a peculiarly opportune time, with the result that to-day we are finding the money and the Grand Trunk Railway keeps the stock. Why will not my right hon. friend, when he has such shining virtues of expression not add to them the still more sterling virtue of keeping to his word after he has pledged it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Grand Trunk was to supply the money to the Grand Trunk Pacific I admit, but does the hon. gentleman believe that under present circumstances this stock could be placed on the market and its value realized? He knows it cannot.
I will answer my Tight hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the answer?

The answer is this. Suppose you say to the Grand Trunk Company: Mr. FOSTER.
' Such was the basis on which you received the $25,000,000 stock, and now you must give to the Grand Trunk Pacific at par th" $10.000,000 which it needs.' If the Grand Trunk Railway would say: 'We are not able at this time to do that "and we would like you to do our hanking,' then the answer of the Prime Minister should be : 'If you cannot put out par for that stock to the extent of the necessity of the Grand Trunk Pacific for this $10,000,000, we will put up the $10.000,000, but you must give us $10,000,000 of that stock.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much better off would we be when we had it?
How much better off?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not a dollar.

The Minister of Finance is .magnificent in his utter disregard of the value of money and security when he is at work for those he wants to help-and who have helped him. In the second place the Minister of Finance is magnificent as a spender.

The Prime Minister has asked if we expected that the Grand Trunk Railway could realize upon this stock at the present time. I will read the language of the right hon. gentleman to be found at page 7688 of ' Hansard,' and then the committee can construe its meaning. The Prime Minister said:
It may be asked, if the aid of the government is to be given only to secure the construction of 75 per cent of the road, where is the company going to get the other 25 per cent. The answer to that is this: that it is provided in the contract that the company shall be authorized to issue a second series of bonds which are to be guaranteed not by the government by the old Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada. May I read here to the House this section, which is an important one.
The Prime Minister read the covenant and followed with this exposition of it:
I need not dwell upon the importance of that covenant on the part of the company. It practically takes away from the guarantee of the government all risk. There is not a dollar to be advanced by the government. We give our credit and nothing else, and our guarantee of 75 cer cent of the construction of the road is to be supplemented by the credit and all the backing of the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself.
As the hon. member for North Toronto says, if they cannot turn that stock over to advantage, let them hand it over to the government or give the government half of it and let us turn it over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To whom?
Let us guarantee it and sell it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Guarantee the stock?

Yes, guarantee it and sell it. Don't we often guarantee the stock of railway companies? If you do not want to dispose of it and raise money on it, raise the money as is now proposed, but let us have a majority of this stock and so let us control the policy of the company so that we can direct the routing of freight as we cannot now. The Prime Minister pointed out then that not only had we the absolute contract that every dollar of that $25,000,000 would be available for constructing the road from time to time as required, but also that the Grand Trunk would guarantee all the bonds beyond the three-quarters guarantee that we were to give and that the country would not be called upon for one dollar.

I wish to read to my right hon. friend another very clear passage, because line upon line and precept upon precept may impress these things on the right hon. gentleman's mind with some force. At page 2483 of the ' Hansard ' of 1904, in regard to the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), he says:
The reason for inserting this condition of the contract last year a as that we wished to prevent speculation in the stock. Well, Mr. Chairman, the Grand Trunk Railway Company must raise money to carry out this enterprise. They cannot build the section from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean simply upon the guarantee of the government, for that will cover only three-quarters of the cost of constructing this part of the road.
Remember that what the Prime Minister said was that the Grand Trunk Company must raise money to carry out this enterprise, not the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the Grand Trunk, which was in it and of it and the whole of it.
And then the equipment of the road is also to be raised from the public, and there are only two manners in which that can be done, either by the issue of bonds, or raising money on their stock. The methods we have adopted will enable them to go into the money market and obtain some money with which to carry on the work. Unless we had done that we would have put them in a position in which they would encounter greater difficulties than they should have to encounter in carrying on an enterprise of this kind.
That carries out exactly the doctrine that was enunciated in the other extract I read to the House, and the country took it so. Now neither the House nor the country can take it so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Why not?

I noticed that twice in this discussion to-day the Prime Minister has harked back to the parallel of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In his last remark he said it was a parallel case and he fully recognized the position of the member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) acknowledging that in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway all these securities were placed in the hands of the government, a first mortgage on the line, the equipment, the steamships, the land and everything they had. These securities were worth nothing in the world's market at that time, but the government advanced money on them. He claimed that this was a parallel case. Let me point out that it would be if his government had not put these most valuable securities, these very branch lines and terminals, out of our power to touch. Every one knows that the Lake Superior branch line and the terminals, and more especially the town sites and other things which this does not cover, would be good securities and that the Canadian Pacific Railway put up securities of that kind. But the right hon. gentleman's government has specifically, in the contract of 1903, exempted all these very things which made the securities put by the Canadian Pacific Railway a real and tangible asset. On his own admission the personal notes and security of the gentlemen interested in the Canadian Pacific Railway were placed at the disposal of the government, whereas here we have the Grand Trunk Townsite Company, formed of Mr. Hays, Mr. Chamberlin, Mr. Wainwright, Mr. Baker and Mr. McHugh, yet none of these gentlemen have offered notes or securities. If we had all these securities there would be no criticism from this side of the House, and, therefore, it becomes all the more necessary that we should at least press for a reasonable share of this stock which hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House think is of no value, but which we think might be of some value.

The legislation of 1904, section 11, to which the Prime Minister referred, as as follows:
The directors of the company elected by the shareholders may make and issue as paid up stock, shares of the common stock of the company, whether subscribed for or not, and may allot and hand over in payment for plant, rolling stock, docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels or materials of any kind, or as considerations for rights, powers, guarantees and privileges acquired, or services rendered, other than promotion services, and also for the bona fide claims of contractors and engineers, such an amount of such common stock as is a fair and bona fide value for the propery purchased, or for the rights, powers, guarantees and privileges acquired.
I would point out that the whole section appears to be clouded purposely as though to lead us to assume that the Grand Trunk was going to give valuable consideration in the shape of plant, rolling stock) docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels, materials of any kind for the $25,000,-

000 common stock which they got from the Grand Trunk Pacific and the only consideration they exacted for that was the guarantee. That is to say they cloud the whole situation by putting in all these words, when no doubt the only intention) was to do as they subsequently did, take over the whole common stock in consideration of guarantees alone. That fully bears out the contention of the hon. member for North Toronto and since that company has got the whole of that common stock-because this section gives the right to transfer the whole of the common stock and I understand they have transferred it for the alleged consideration of $203,000-1 would ask the Finance Minister whether or not he knows if that $203,000 includes any promotion services because this section expressly forbids promotion services being a consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gave the House the information I got from the company.
Does the minister know?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not answer.

If there is, it is an express contravention of this section. I think the suggestion of the hon member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) is a very good one, especially in view of the fact that the company have paid at the most only $203,000 for this $25,000,000 worth of stock. The Finance Minister does not think that this is a valuable security but I point out that under the present arrangement, in case default is made in payment of the bonds which the government have guaranteed, the only remedy we have under that section is to take possession of the road, and when it becomes a paying concern hand it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific again. So soon as it becomes a bankrupt concern and does not pay its way, it is: saddled upon the country. If we have the common stock we can pay the bonds of the company and being the owner of the common stock we would be the Grand Trunk Pacific and have control of the whole situation. In that way we could become the absolute owner of the road subject only to the payment of interest. If we become owners of the common stock and control the company we get a tangible security because we get rid of this onerous condition of having to hand over the road when it is paying. If we had the stock we would be masters of the situation, and if the road did not pay could become absolute owners of it.
Could the Finance Minister give any definite knowledge of what the Grand Trunk Pacific were offered for these bonds which they could not sell?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A price offered by whom?
By the brokers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I expressed the opinion that the bonds could be placed at about 90, and did not base it on any actual transaction, but on my knowledge of the money market.

If the sole purpose of this Bill is to relieve the money situation of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the extent of $10,000,000, why would not the Finance Minister take up $10,000,000 of their bonds as part security and give them the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am happy to have that suggestion. That is the exact purpose of this legislation :
On section 3,
The issue of bonds to be made by the company hereunder shall be for a principal amount not exceeding ten million dollars, and shall be secured, subject to any prior lien or charge, by a mortgage or deed of trust by way of mortgage of the said prairie section and of the undertaking, equipment and property, tolls, rights and franchises of the company described in the said mortgage, and shall be guaranteed as to the payment of the principal and interest thereof by the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada (hereinafter called the ' Grand Trunk Company').

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The security of that guarantee is a very remote one, as has already been pointed out more than once. The company has other securities which it might give. I shall not allude again to what has been said just now with regard to the advisability of securing stock of the company to be held until its loan is repaid; but there are other assets of the company which might very well be included in the mortgage. Let me allude to two of them. One is the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific in a corporation which has secured a great number of town sites, namely, the Grand Trunk Pacific Townsite and Development Company. I understand that the Grand Trunk Pacific practically owns the whole of the stock in that company which has received very favourable terms from the government having been permitted to acquire a very large amount of land in .western Canada at an exceedingly low rate. There is no reason why that stock, aggregating about $3,000,000, should not be pledged as security for this loan. Then there is another asset which might be very well pledged to the government, particularly in view of the discussion which we have had this evening, and that is the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the Port Arthur branch. No doubt that branch is already covered by a mortgage and of course I would not suggest that we should do anything which would in the slightest degree displace the security of that mortgage. But the Grand Trunk Pacific has

an equity in that branch as I understand it. It has an interest subject to that mortgage. Why should we .not take security upon that branch? I understand it is practically completed. A hen upon it would be of the greatest possible benefit to the government. Why is it that these two items of very considerable value- more partcularlv. perhaps, future than present value, although the interests in the town sites must be very valuable even at present,-are not included in the mortgage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our judgment is that that mortgage upon the property, remote thotigh it may be, and the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway, which has an established value on the market, are adequate security for this loan, and additional securities are not required to protect the public interest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is a fourth mortgage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not exactly a fourth mortgage, but a fourth lien. There is one intervening, but not in the form of a mortgage.	-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What will be the total value of the liens ahead of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say now, but I gave it at an earlier stage, to the best of my judgment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Well, in making a loan, it is desirable to have the security absolutely unquestioned. The pledging of these securities to make good this loan would be no detriment to the company and it would be of importance to the people.
On section 4,
4. The company, in addition to any powers which it now has in such behalf, is empowered to make such mortgage or deed of trust, and to create and issue the bonds contemplated by this Act, and the power of the company in such behalf shall not be deemed to be limited by the provisions of section 13 of chaper 122 of the statutes of 1903.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Finance Minister referred to the enormous assistance which the Grand Trunk Railway had given this enterprise. We know that in consideration of that assistance, the Grand Trunk Pacific has handed over to the Grand Trunk Railway $25,000,000 in common stock. If the assistance given by the Grand Trunk Railway is large, that given by the country is enormously larger. My hon friend spoke of this contract as if it were somewhat an unfavourable one to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Let me point out that his own colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir Richard Cartwright, said in 1903, page 9361 of ' Hansard
I believe that a really good bargain may be one which is to the ad -antage of both parties. I think this is undoubtedly an instance of that sort.
He thus makes the distinct statement that this contract was eminently to the advantage of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway as well. In 1904 that contract was modified. Let me read what Mr. Alfred Smither who is a very able and influential member of the directorate of the Grand Trunk Railway, said:
Comparing the agreement of 1904 with that of 1902-3, that which we present to you to-day is a much more favourable agreement.
Therefore, the agreement of 1903, according to the declaration of the Minister of Trade and Commerce was one to the advantage of both parties, and the agreement of 1904, according to Mr. Smither, was still more favourable to the company. It cannot then be well said that this is a particularly burdensome agreement so far as the Grand Trunk Railway is concerned. The Grand Trunk Railway gets $25,000,000 of common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific in consideration of the assistance which it gives to this enterprise. The country is giving to the same enterprise ten times as much assistance. Why not declare at this juncture. that, in consideration of the assistance this country is contributing to the enterprise, we shall have an absolute transfer to the government, in trust for the people, of not less than $10,000,000 of the stock of that company. The common stock has already been issued, the preference stock still remains. One is more valuable for investment purposes, or will be in the future, and the other for purely speculative purposes. But, if the assistance given by the Grand Trunk Railway Company calls for a transfer to them of $25,000,000 of the common stock, why does not the assistance given by the country, which is tenfold greater, justify handing over to the country $10,000,000 of the preference stock? The Minister of Finance says it is of no value. Put on the market to-day it may be of no value. Twenty-five million dollars of the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway had no value in 1882 or 1884. But, if the government had, even with the conditions of the western country at that time, asked that in consideration of the assistance given, twenty or twenty-five million dollars of the common stock of the Canadian Pacific should be handed over to the government, cannot we see what a tremendous asset that would be in the coffers of the government at the present time? So, looking to the future, and not to the immediate present, and realizing that the security of the government in respect of this loan and these guarantees rests upon the success of this enterprise, realizing that we

are taking so great a share of the risk, whatever it may be of this enterprise, are not the people of this country honestly entitled to some share in its success if it shall be, as we hope it may be, a great success in the no distant future.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is going over the same ground as my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mt. Foster). I can only repeat the argument

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That was with regard to pledging it, I undei stood.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is as to the profit to be derived from this common stock. The hen. gentleman says that, as we are contributing much more than the Grand Trunk Railway Company, we should have an interest in the common stock. I think that the contribution of the Grand Trunk by way of aid is enormously greater than the proportion he has occasionally indicated. However, we need not dwell upon that now. Whatever the grant is, they get for it only a second mortgage, while the government, for every dollar it puts in by way of its own guarantee, gets a first mortgage and is en-tirc-ly protected.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not understand that the Grand Trunk get a second mortgage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. minister is describing the case precisely as it was under the contract of 1903, but he has not described the conditions of the contract of 1904. Under the contracts of 1904, if default of interest shall be made, the government stand precisely on the same footing as the Grand Trunk. A receiver is to be put in charge, the road operated and the surplus earnings given to the government and to the Grand Trunk in proportion to the bonds they are guaranteeing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The effect of the legislation of 1904 was not to vary our first mortgage, but to provide that we might postpone the remedy for a certain time. We have, as I understand it, a first mortgage, whereas the Grand Trunk has only a second mortgage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The only remedy provided under the legislation of 1904 is to put a receiver in charge, operate the road and hand over the surplus earnings to the two parties according to the amount of bonds they have guaranteed. I am speaking of the condition in case of default of interest; but that is the essential point, for if the road is operated for fifty years, or whatever the term may be, without default of interest, there would be no question as to first or second mortgage. The essential feature is, what is to be done in case of default of interest ? In that case, the Mr. FIELDING.
Grand Trunk is on precisely the same footing as the government. So, while the government has nominally a first mortgage, it has not a first mortgage in fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For a limited time there would be that distribution. But I think the hon. member will find that, while reserving to ourselves a first mortgage, for a limited time the receiver is appointed and the net receipts distributed pro rata. But our first mortgage remains. The hon. member's argument is that our remedy is only in default of interest and that practically we do not have a first mortgage. But that is only for a limited time-we postpone foreclosure for the time. I speak from recollection.

The effect of the legislation is that, for the first seven years, they do not pay interest at all. For three years thereafter they are allowed to capitalize it, and then we are not allowed to do anything for a period of five years. All mortgages are alike until there is default. But, under the 1904 contract 'with the Grand Trunk Pacific on default, the Toad is put into the hands of a receiver and the net receipts are divided between the parties in proporton to their claims against the road- 75 per cent to the government in respect of its guarantees and 25 per cent to the Grand Trunk. What does that mean? It means that we have no preference. If we had a first mortgage, we could take everything and the Grand Trunk get nothing. But as the net receipts are divided * pari passu,' it is not a first mortgage because other mortgages would not be entitled to one cent until our claim was paid in full if it were a first mortgage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What the minister (Mr. Fielding) has in mind is that for a period of five years no rights shall be ex-exercised-default for less than five years does not entitle the goverinment to take action. But, if there is default for over five years, then the government may enter into possession and a receiver be appointed, and, in that case, the government and the Grand Trunk stand upon the same footing.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think that, to a large extent, my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) is right. The other day, in discussing the matter, an hon. member left an impression on my mind that by the legislation of 1904 we placed ourselves in such a position that during the whole of these five years the holder of the second mortgage could practically step in and do anything he liked. I looked it up, and I find that that is an erroneous view. At no time can the second mortgagee step in ahead of our mortgage. But, after five years, the division will be on the basis of 75 per cent to the government and 25 per cent to the Grand Trunk.

Practically we were turned into trustees by the contract of 1904. We had an ordinary first mortgage, but in 1904 it was provided that, in default'of interest, a receiver should be appointed who should distribute the proceeds in the way mentioned. As soon as they caught up on the interest, the property would go back into the possession of the company. As a matter of fact, we can never take possession of the road permanently.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would like the Bill to remain in committee, in case we should have any further suggestions.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Bill (No. 98) to amend the Exchequer Court Act-Mr. Aylesworth-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The whole purpose of this Act is to define anew the status of the registrar of the Exchequer Court. Two years ago an Act was passed with regard to the salary of the registrar of the court, fixing the salary of the present incumbent of the office at $3,000 per annum. As that was a special piece of legislation, it has been considered in accordance with the ordinary rule of interpretation of statutes that the provisions of the special Act would have force and effect instead of the provisions of the general Act with Tegard to the Civil Service which was passed last session, and the result would be that the position of the registrar of the Exchequer Court would be defined by the terms of the special Act of 1907 instead of falling under the provisions of the general Act with regard to the Civil Service of 1908. The whole purpose of this Bill is to place the present registrar and any future registrar of the Exchequer Court, under the provisions of the general Civil Service Act of last session. It will be observed that in the second subsection of section 2, it is provided that the registrar shall rank as an officer of subdivision A of the first division of the inside service, in or under the Department of Justice. That would be the position to which, in virtue of his salary of $3,000 per annum, the registrar would have been placed in the classification under the Act of last session if that statute had applied to his case. The whole purpose of this legislation, as I say, is to accomplish that result, and have the general provisions of the Civil Service Act apply to the registrar of the Exchequer Court instead of the provisions of the special Act of two years ago.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Resolved, that it is expedient to establish tlie Department of Labour as a separate department of the Civil Service of Canada, with a Minister of Labour in charge of such department, who shall be paid a salary of $7,000 per annum; and that the Governor in Council may appoint in addition to the present staff of the Department of Labour one adi-tional clerk in the said department at a salary of $1,000 per annum, and a private secretary to the minister at a salary of $600 per annum.-Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That all the words after ' per annum J in the 3rd line be omitted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As this is merely preliminary to the Bill I have no objection in letting the resolution pass on the understanding that any discussion which might ordinarily take place will take place upon the Bill in committee.

Yes.
